# Glossary

Before linkage
:   Before any outcome is linked to a text.

Catalogue
:   The delivered story texts.

Cell
:   Within a language, the texts of one reading level and one origin, generated or classic.

Components
:   The three text properties that the confirmatory models test, LexicalDifficulty, GrammaticalLoad and ReferentialContinuity. The anchors of each are the features that identify it.

Extract
:   The reading sessions that the data controller, also called the provider, holds until in-principle acceptance.

F1
:   The harmonic mean of precision and recall, in points from 0 to 100.

Fixed sample
:   A sample of 2,000 story versions per language, chosen by a fixed pseudo-random function of the story identifier (a keyed hash), so that every run draws the same versions.

Noise-only reliability
:   $\rho^2$, the share of a score's variance that is not measurement noise (Measurement error and calibration).

Served text
:   The exact version of a story that the app showed a child.

Translated benchmark
:   Public English children's stories translated one sentence at a time, so that every sentence boundary of each translation is known.

Transport
:   Carrying a constant estimated on the treebanks' genres over to the stories.

Treebank
:   A corpus of sentences annotated by hand with their grammatical structure, from which a parser learns to assign that structure to new text. Universal Dependencies (UD) treebanks share one scheme and are usually divided into training, development and test sets for learning, tuning and evaluation. The parallel PUD treebanks annotate the same 1,000 news and Wikipedia sentences in many languages. Of these, 750 were written in English and 250 in German, French, Italian or Spanish, and the translations into the other languages went through English.

# S1. The theory object

The object is a single machine-readable file, `theory/intract.theory.yaml`, which the theoryforge package reads and checks [@bernabeuTheoryforge2026]. From this file, `theory/make_nomological_net.R` draws Figure 2 of the main text. Running `theory/build_theory.R` reproduces the checklist scores, the redundancy screen and the implications reported below, and `theory/check_manuscript_claims.R` prints the counts quoted here.

The object registers sixteen constructs and thirty-three propositions linking them, each with a mechanism and a direction, thirty as directed edges of the causal graph and three as moderation claims. Six auxiliary assumptions are recorded as separate entries, five of them corresponding to questions put to the data controller (Table 2 of the main text). Seven of the object's ten predictions are marked diagnostic against one of the six rival accounts it names.

The rigour checklist scores the object at 91.9 out of 100, and all twelve items pass. On falsifiability and precision, at least one prediction forbids an observation, all ten are interval predictions, and their mean severity exceeds the checklist's threshold. For construct quality, every construct has a definition, an intended measurement and boundary conditions, no pair is flagged by the lexical redundancy screen (largest observed similarity 0.17), and the theory's scope is stated. Every proposition states a mechanism, at least one relation is causal, and every prediction is reachable from a proposition in the graph. Auxiliary assumptions are fewer than propositions, and none was added defensively in response to a prediction. Finally, at least one prediction discriminates between registered alternatives, and the formal-model entry refers to the design specification used for the precision analysis.

Because the causal graph is acyclic, it yields sixty-one testable implications, of which the main text's fourth outcome-neutral quality check tests three. The most consequential is that the three text properties should be mutually independent given the reading level, the generation route, the story's content and its translation. The quality of that translation is unmeasured, and the fourth check states the proxy that stands in for it. A first version of the object, without the text-provenance construct, implied that they were independent unconditionally. That implication is false of any real corpus, because a text's target reading level shifts all three property families at once. Adding text provenance as a common cause of all three, with an incoming path from the reader's decoding automaticity, corrected the implication and produced the adjustment set the analysis uses.

The third tested implication is that the difficulty rating should carry no further information about reading level given reading time. The literature gives more specific grounds for expecting it to fail than for the other two. A reported feeling of difficulty is a metacognitive experience drawing on affective as well as cognitive input [@efklidesMetacognitionAffectWhat2006]. When 274 pupils of grades 7 to 9 solved mathematical problems, that feeling varied across the phases of a task and bore on performance only indirectly, through ideas about what the task required [@efklidesFeelingDifficultyAspect1999]. After a battery of cognitive tasks, 80 children aged 8 to 12, 38 with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, rated task difficulty and effort. The ratings were uncorrelated with each other and only weakly related to performance [@torresMetacognitiveRatingsCognitive2026]. Among college readers, such judgements often rest on surface features of a text, which are poor cues to comprehension [@thiedePoorMetacomprehensionAccuracy2010]. The main text's fourth quality check states which omitted path a failure of this implication would identify and how that path would be reported.

# S2. Studies from the accompanying systematic review

Two tables list the studies closest to the present design in method and in modality. Those closest in method, in @tbl-computational-reading, entered a broad set of text features into a statistical or machine-learning model to predict a behavioural or comprehension outcome in children.

```{=latex}
\begingroup\small
```

| **Study** | **Sample and design** | **Method and key findings** |
|---|---|---|
| @pickrenContributionTextCharacteristics2022 | Children (*N* = 158, ages 8;8 to 11;2); multilevel logistic models | Word frequency, pronoun density, concreteness and deep cohesion each predicted passage comprehension after decoding and language comprehension were controlled, and lexical arousal predicted it beyond those. The text features varied across only 11 passages. |
| @aparicioComprehensionPerformancesExplanatory2022 | Children (*N* = 1,229, grades 2 to 9); multivariate regression | Text and sentence characteristics predicted comprehension, but the direction and size of each effect varied by question type. |
| @ludewigVocabularyTextCoverage2023 | Children (*N* = 924, grade 4); non-linear regression | Estimated lexical text coverage predicted comprehension non-linearly, rising more steeply once coverage exceeded about 56 per cent. |
| @yuyangniePredictingReadingComprehension2022 | Elementary-school students; feature-based prediction model | Sentence complexity, lexical surprisal and rare-word features improved prediction of item-level comprehension scores over a baseline. |
| @wasitokiranaSentenceProcessingIndonesianEnglish2025 | Bilingual children (*N* = 44, 22 with language impairment); eye-tracking | Syntactic complexity impaired comprehension accuracy and slowed recall, disproportionately for children with language impairment. |

# S3. Language resources for the text features

We set out the reasons for the first rule under Materials and the limits of the uniform resources, then register the pipeline settings and diagnostics the fourth rule requires. @tbl-resources lists each feature family's resources for the ten languages of the structural sample (Section S8), and the paragraphs after it treat Korean, the placement of every language not in the classification of orthographic depth used in the main text, and Greek. @tbl-resources-more and the rules after it extend the same design to the app's nine other languages, and a paragraph on adult-rated affective values follows them. The story texts delivered on 26 October 2026 hold none of four of those nine, Indonesian, Romanian, Russian and Thai, and add Bulgarian, Hungarian, Kazakh and Serbian, whose resources will be registered here before submission.<!-- PENDING: P81 --> The section ends with three subsections. The first two set out how the pipeline is validated without human annotation and how measurement error in the component scores is estimated and corrected. The third registers the rules that decide whether a third parser joins the two-parser mean.

A multilingual design faces a measurement problem that a monolingual one does not. Concreteness scores from a 40,000-item English rating study, a 350,000-lemma German regression, a 1,400-item Spanish rating study and a 77-language embedding prediction are four different measurements under one label. If each language's resource is chosen for its local quality, the method of measurement is perfectly confounded with language. Standardising within language removes differences in location and scale but not in construct. One coherent approach uses a single uniformly produced resource everywhere, accepting lower absolute quality for higher comparability. The other uses native norms and treats every cross-language comparison as descriptive. We choose uniformity of specification, because language enters the confirmatory models as a grouping factor with varying slopes, and those slopes must mean the same thing in every language. Bias from measures that target different constructs, or that differ in metric across groups, puts cross-group inferences in doubt [@boerDetectingSystematicMeasurement2018], whereas unequal random error can be corrected and bounded. That is why the first rule under Materials fixes the specification once for every language, and why the subsections on validation and measurement error correct and bound the random error that remains. The same reasoning keeps concreteness and age of acquisition out of the pooled lexical solution, since only native norms, which measure them differently in each language, are admissible as their primary resource. A resource predicted by one procedure in every language enters only their separate pooled sensitivity solutions. The native-norm sensitivity analysis under Materials shows how much the choice of resource matters.

The rules under Materials exclude two widely used resources, each the obvious candidate for its family, so we record why. The `wordfreq` package is not the primary frequency source. Its data are a frozen snapshot of usage to about 2021, and its maintainer discontinued it in September 2024 to avoid ingesting post-2022 web text contaminated by generated language. Its Korean and Greek wordlists draw on fewer sources than the rest. It serves only as an independent list in the third gate on the frequency lists (Validation without human annotation). The non-English editions of the NRC Valence, Arousal and Dominance lexicon are not used at all. Each of their values is an English rating copied in 2022 to a machine translation of the word, which the second rule under Materials excludes, and their licence is non-commercial. MEmoLon's training targets were also English ratings carried over by translation. Its released values, however, are predictions from a model fitted within each language on word representations learned from that language's own text [@buechelLearningEvaluatingEmotion2020], the case the second rule admits.

The primary frequency resource is a set of 19 lists built for this study from the 2024 release of the OpenSubtitles corpus [@tiedemannOpenSubtitles2024MassivelyParallel2026]. One deposited script builds them, counting in each language the unit in which its texts are looked up. Subtitle frequencies predicted word recognition better than written-corpus frequencies, or explained variance beyond them, in American and British English, French and Chinese [@brysbaertMovingKuceraFrancis2009; @newUseFilmSubtitles2007; @caiSUBTLEXCHChineseWord2010; @vanheuvenSubtlexUKNewImproved2014]. A subtitle collection is also the only source that one documented pipeline can count identically in all 19 varieties. The published subs2vec lists [@vanparidonSubs2vecWordEmbeddings2021], which their download script builds from the 2018 raw release of the same corpus, are not used, because they count lower-cased whitespace tokens. Their Korean list therefore holds eojeols, content words with their particles or endings attached, and their Arabic and Hebrew lists hold words with their clitics attached. They include no Chinese or Thai list. The new lists use no story text, so they are built before submission. They are deposited with their counts, corpus sizes and title manifests but no subtitle text, and with the attribution the corpus requires [@lisonOpenSubtitles2016ExtractingLarge2016]. <!-- PENDING: P48 -->

Each list samples one variety's raw files, the Brazilian files for the provider's Portuguese. It keeps files whose language-identification confidence is at least .90 and one file per film or episode, from release years 1900 to 2022. Most 2024 files carry no upload date, so that window only approximates a corpus that predates large language models. Titles are drawn in a fixed pseudo-random order until a list holds 100 million lookup units, which gives every language a standard error of about 0.04 on the Zipf scale (base-10 log frequency per billion words) at the rare-word threshold. Lists and texts share one normalisation function and the frozen tokenisers, and frequencies are expressed as Zipf values with Laplace smoothing [@vanheuvenSubtlexUKNewImproved2014]. In mean log frequency, a non-name content token absent from the list takes the smoothed floor value, since discarding zero-frequency words is the weaker rule [@brysbaertDealingZeroWord2013]. The mean over matched tokens alone is a sensitivity analysis. Lists built by the same script from the 2018 release [@lisonOpenSubtitles2018StatisticalRescoring2018], which predates large language models, are the sensitivity resource, and their per-language correlations with the primary lists are reported.

The rare-word share defined under Materials uses a threshold of Zipf 4, ten per million, for three reasons. On 2,000 public children's stories from the TinyStories corpus, which a language model wrote [@eldanTinyStoriesHowSmall2023], a threshold of Zipf 3 left 56 per cent of stories with no rare content token. The share's split-half reliability was then .54, against .74 at Zipf 4. At Zipf 4, the share stayed distinct from mean frequency (*r* = -.59), and its agreement with English across the parallel PUD treebanks rose from .31 to .59 in French. The range in which frequency matters also depends on a reader's exposure [@brysbaertWordFrequencyEffect2018], which is smaller in children than in adults. Counting absent tokens as rare agreed with English at least as well as discarding them in 9 of 10 languages. In inflecting languages, however, a share counted on word forms at Zipf 4 partly measures inflection. Given the English source's share, its partial correlation with the inflection rate is about .4 in Spanish, French, Italian, Polish, Russian and Turkish, against about .1 at Zipf 3. An inflection diagnostic is therefore computed on the translated benchmark before submission and on the catalogue's fixed sample after acceptance, and it is reported beside the lexical slopes. The shares at Zipf 3 and over matched tokens alone are sensitivity analyses. <!-- PENDING: P63 -->

Subtitles transcribe spoken film and television, whereas many words in the books children read from age 7 never occur on British television [@korochkinaChildrenYoungPeoples2024]. The register mismatch for developing readers is a limitation that no available uniform resource removes, but its size can be measured. On the same 2,000 public stories, frequency from adult subtitles ranked texts almost exactly as frequency from the subtitles of the British children's channel CBBC did (*r* = .953). The CBBC frequencies, and those of the preschool channel CBeebies, come from SUBTLEX-UK [@vanheuvenSubtlexUKNewImproved2014]. Adult subtitle frequency agreed less with the books read at ages 7 to 9 in the Children and Young People's Books Lexicon, CYP-LEX (*r* = .80), and with CBeebies (*r* = .789). CBBC itself agreed with those books less than adult subtitles did (*r* = .757). Corpus size does not explain this. Over the books' vocabulary, CBBC holds 13.4 million tokens, the books 11.2 million and CBeebies 5.7 million. The main gap therefore lies between spoken and written language, and filtering subtitles by genre would not close it. After acceptance and before linkage, a register diagnostic measures the gap on the catalogue. Within reading level, it correlates each English source text's mean Zipf under the 2024 list with its mean under CYP-LEX, in the bands for ages 7 to 9 and 10 to 12. The same diagnostic runs in every language with a native child-register norm, such as the Chinese children's lexicon of oral words, CCLOOW [@liCCLOOWChineseChildrens2024]. Of the values derived from CYP-LEX, only these correlations are deposited, since no licence to redistribute derived statistics was found.

The evidence does not all point one way. A recent study found that frequency estimates from a large-language-model corpus prompted for child-directed text fitted young German readers better than child-book norms did [@schepensCanLargeLanguage2025]. Generated corpora, however, are neither frozen nor documented in the way a subtitle pipeline is, and the same study notes that they show atypical linguistic patterns. A pooled analysis of five self-paced reading studies in German found that a written-corpus database fitted sentential reading times best in most models, ahead of subtitle frequencies, although predictability effects dwarfed those of frequency. The ranking of databases also differed by participant population [@haeuserNotSubtlexWord2025]. In Chinese, the lexicon of children's screen language correlated particularly well with frequencies from children's books [@liCCLOOWChineseChildrens2024]. These findings are a further reason for the native-norm sensitivity analysis. They caution against interpreting a pooled frequency coefficient as a property of the language when it is partly a property of the resource.

Contextual diversity, the number of documents in which a word occurs, explained naming and lexical-decision times better than frequency [@adelmanContextualDiversityNot2006; @brysbaertMovingKuceraFrancis2009], although its interpretation as contextual variability is disputed [@hollisDelineatingLinguisticContexts2020]. It is counted in the same pass as frequency. A lookup unit's value is $\log_{10}[(d + 1)/(D + 1)]$, where $d$ is the number of sampled films whose subtitle file contains it and $D$ the number of films in the language's sample. The contextual-diversity refit under Sensitivity analyses replaces the mean-frequency anchor with the token-weighted mean of these values over the same tokens, and each language's text-level correlation between the two is reported. Before submission, the per-language correlation matrices of the lexical features and their split-half values, labelled as internal consistency, are published from the translated benchmark. <!-- PENDING: P62 --> On the catalogue before linkage, the agreement of LexicalDifficulty across alternative resources is reported beside the slopes. The pairs compared are the 2024 and 2018 lists, the 1 GB and 100 MB surprisal models, and the two parsers' lemmas for diversity and density.

The register problem extends to surprisal. In a study of German expository reading, language models whose training matched the reader's experience fitted late reading measures better than general-corpus models did [@skrjanecLanguageModelsMatch2026]. No child-register model exists for these languages under one procedure, so the mismatch is recorded as a limitation of the uniform primary resource, the Goldfish models. Their 1 GB tier is chosen on the psychometric grounds given in @tbl-resources. The 100 MB tier, trained with the same tokeniser on the same stream with a tenth of the data, enters a registered sensitivity refit. On 300 public TinyStories, English text means from the two tiers correlated at *r* = .886 (95 per cent interval .859 to .908), the starting expectation for their agreement. To measure the mismatch, we will report each model's mean per-word surprisal on the story texts, after acceptance and before linkage, and on a held-out 10 MB sample of its training corpus, OSCAR 21.09. The ratio of the two, reported with them, expresses the register gap on a scale comparable across languages and flags any language where the model is badly matched. None of these quantities involves an outcome.

Before submission, both tiers and the multilingual contrast are tested on open adult eye-tracking data in the study's own languages. The two waves of the Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus, MECO [@siegelmanExpandingHorizonsCrosslinguistic2022; @siegelmanWave2Multilingual2025], cover 13 of the 19 versions: Dutch, English, German, Greek, Hebrew, Italian, Korean, Russian, Spanish, Turkish, both Chinese scripts and Brazilian Portuguese. For each, the check computes the gain in log-likelihood from word surprisal for gaze duration and for total reading time, under each model. The 1 GB tier stays primary unless the 100 MB tier gives the larger gain for total reading time in a majority of the overlapping languages. MECO's Traditional-script sample also compares the conversion route registered for Traditional Chinese with Goldfish's native Traditional-script model. Every result is reported here as validation in adult readers. <!-- PENDING: P49 -->

Several properties of the surprisal pipeline are registered here because the fourth rule requires them to be frozen. Each text is scored in windows of 512 tokens, the model's maximum, each beginning with the start token `[CLS]` as in training and never ending with `[SEP]`. Windows advance by 256 tokens, and the last one ends at the text's final token. Each token's surprisal is taken from the first window that contains it, so every token after the first window is scored with at least 255 tokens of preceding context. Goldfish marks the beginning of a word, so a summed subword surprisal credits part of one word's ending to the next. Word surprisal therefore takes the correction of @pimentelHowComputeProbability2024, with `[SEP]` in the set of boundary tokens. The correction telescopes, so text means without names barely move (*r* = .9995), but each word's value becomes a proper probability. A similar correction fitted naturalistic reading times less well [@ohLeadingWhitespacesLanguage2024], although the two versions barely differ at the level of a text mean. A fixed table replaces characters that a language's tokeniser cannot encode, such as the em dash (U+2014) in 10 of the 18 tokenisers, with equivalents in its vocabulary. A word that still holds an unknown token leaves the mean. In Chinese and Thai, 15 to 43 per cent of segmenter word boundaries fall inside a Goldfish token. A token that straddles two words is then split between them in proportion to their characters. That split is a heuristic that stands in for exact character-level marginalisation [@giulianelliProperTreatmentTokenization2024]. Its agreement of *r* ≥ .999 was measured against another heuristic, so its error against the exact marginal is unknown. Per language, we will report the mean and maximum subword-token count per text, the tokens-per-word ratio, the replacement counts and the proportion of texts longer than one window.

The date of the Goldfish training snapshot favours this study, because OSCAR 21.09 derives from the February 2021 Common Crawl, which predates the generator that wrote these stories. A predictability model that could not have been fitted to text of this kind is a safeguard, whereas the same frozen-snapshot property counted against `wordfreq` as a measure of current usage. The multilingual contrast shares the property, since the training data of XGLM-4.5B end in March or April 2020 [@linFewshotLearningMultilingual2022]. EuroLLM-1.7B serves the contrast only as a fallback, partly for this reason. Its report lists, for the last 10 per cent of pre-training, Cosmopedia-v2, a synthetic corpus of textbooks, blog posts and stories written by a language model [@martinsEuroLLMMultilingualLanguage2024], and it lacks Hebrew, Indonesian and Thai. The classic stories, however, are based on public-domain tales, and they may echo wording that the training corpus contains. A model's surprisal is lower on text it has seen than on text it has not. A classic text's lexical component would then be pulled towards the easy end for a reason unrelated to the child. The per-language comparison of classic and generated surprisal, registered under Sensitivity analyses, checks for this bias. The refit on generated texts alone shows how far the bias could affect the estimates.

The fourth rule also requires sentence segmentation to be registered in full. Before any stage runs, each text is normalised once to Unicode normalisation form NFC and stripped of invisible format characters, and its pages are joined with one space. English is segmented by Segment any Text [@frohmannSegmentAnyText2024], the `sat-12l-sm` model run through `wtpsplit` 2.2.2 [@segmentanytextWtpsplit2026] at a threshold of .25, with no boundary after a colon. A colon that introduces speech is the model's one systematic error, and that rule removes it at no cost. In the 18 translations, the union segmenter keeps every sentence end the translation marks itself and takes the others from its English source. Thai does not, in general, mark sentence ends with punctuation [@minixhoferWheresPointSelfsupervised2023], and its annotation guidelines record no consensus on where sentences end [@boonkwanAnnotationGuidelineLST202020]. In a recent Arabic benchmark, 39 per cent of boundaries carried no sentence-final punctuation, and 24 per cent in children's texts [@elkholyArabicSentenceSegmentation2026]. Neural machine translation has until recently translated sentence by sentence [@marufSurveyDocumentlevelNeural2022], so the English source's sentence ends can be projected onto each translation. Machine-translation evaluation likewise transfers a reference's segment boundaries to unsegmented output [@matusovEvaluatingMachineTranslation2005], and cross-lingual work projects annotation across aligned texts [@yarowskyInducingMultilingualText2001].

For the projection, the same model runs on the translation, and its boundary probability is kept at each character. Candidates are the characters that end a whitespace token, are punctuation or have a boundary probability of at least $10^{-5}$, and a colon is never one. For an English source of $m$ sentences, an exact Viterbi search chooses $m - 1$ increasing candidates. It maximises the summed log-odds of the chosen boundaries plus a length term for each target segment. That term is the log-likelihood of the segment's length under a normal model centred on its English sentence's length, scaled by the text's own length ratio [@galeProgramAligningSentences1993]. The variance of that model is estimated per language on the development portion of FLORES-200's professionally translated articles [@nllbteamScalingNeuralMachine2024], and no weight is tuned. Where the structural counts (Section S7) confirm that a translation's pages match its English source's, the search runs page by page. The union segmenter then adds every boundary of the registered model on the translation that falls at a terminal mark (sentence-final punctuation), skipping closing quotation marks. A text with fewer candidates than projected boundaries has its sentence-based features declared missing. If the delivery carries the provider's per-sentence length arrays, those arrays give the boundaries in every translation. Pure projection is a sensitivity analysis, with Segment any Text alone reported beside it. Both parsers, the word function, the dialogue spans and every sentence-based feature take these sentences, and the code, the variances and the boundary offsets are deposited. A title is the first line of a text or page if it has at most eight words and no sentence-final mark. Titles are identified on the English source and carried to each translation by line index if line structure survives.

A sentence of a translated text therefore ends wherever the translation writes a sentence-final mark, and wherever its rendering of one English source sentence ends. Where a translation marks no end itself, as in Thai, or omits one, as in some Arabic units, the English source decides, with the consequences for sentence counts stated under Materials. Errors in segmenting the English source are thereby shared by every translation. No adapter, large language model or language-specific segmenter is registered in any role. A fine-tuned adapter would give one language its own model, which the first rule under Materials does not allow, and in domain it lifts Thai by only 0.8 points [@frohmannSegmentAnyText2024, Table 2]. Segmenters built on large language models cannot be reproduced through a hosted interface, and on song lyrics they altered 1.5 to 2 per cent of input characters despite instructions not to [@frohmannSegmentAnyText2024]. They also under-segment Arabic [@elkholyArabicSentenceSegmentation2026]. Thai- and Arabic-specific segmenters learn native conventions with different notions of a sentence, such as the joining of clauses that share a subject [@boonkwanAnnotationGuidelineLST202020], so their counts would not be comparable across languages.

Per language, we will report the mean and standard deviation of sentence length and the proportion of sentences ending without a terminal mark. For every text, we will report the ratios of its sentences and of its terminal marks to those of its English source, with their median, interquartile range and share within 10 per cent. These diagnostics decide nothing. The checks that can remove a language's sentence-based features are set out under Validation without human annotation.

The two parsers of the grammatical features are Stanza 1.15.0 in its `nocharlm` tier, which tracks release 2.18 of Universal Dependencies, and UDPipe 2 with its models of release 2.17 [@instituteofformalandappliedlinguisticsUDPipe2Models2025]. The `nocharlm` packages are those built without a character language model. Both run on every sentence of every text, each with the registered treebank for the language and its own tokeniser, and Serbian text is parsed through its Latin transliteration (the fifth script rule below). A uniform encoder, the pretrained network that represents a parser's input, does not give uniform quality [@wuAreAllLanguages2020], so reliability is measured per language. On hand-annotated text, the parsers' text-level errors correlated .31 to .76. Diverse base parsers matter more than the combination model, and in reparsing [@sagaeParserCombinationReparsing2006], unweighted voting performs essentially as well as learned weights [@surdeanuEnsembleModelsDependency2010]. Equal weights also avoid estimating a parameter per language [@dawesRobustBeautyImproper1979]. On the hand-annotated text of release 2.18, with paired cluster-bootstrap intervals, which resample whole documents, the mean was never materially worse than the better single parser. It was significantly better than Stanza alone in 13 of 15 conditions, the two Thai conditions excepted. GrammaticalLoad's reliability against hand annotation rose, for example, from .879 to .921 on Hebrew IAHLTwiki and from .770 to .825 on Simplified Chinese GSDSimp. Before submission, both parsers run on all 19 registered test sets and the parallel PUD treebanks with paired intervals. <!-- PENDING: P47 --> A unit longer than 100 words takes Stanza's parse in both members of the mean. UDPipe 2 failed on 3 of the 5 Arabic units over 150 words, whereas Stanza tracked the hand annotation above that length. The share of such units is reported per language, a language above 1 per cent is flagged, and the calibration applies the same rule. UDPipe 2 runs on a GPU with deterministic operations, and it moves to a CPU if a rerun of the pilot on 1 per cent of the catalogue does not reproduce identical output.

Treebanks annotate the same structures differently [@berdicevskisUsingUniversalDependencies2018], so the counting rules are fixed on syntactic words after multi-word-token expansion. Open clausal complements are not counted as clauses, because they make up 9.8 to 12.0 per cent of clause heads in eight treebanks but 0.3 to 0.9 per cent in Turkish IMST and Arabic PADT. Standardising within language cannot remove a convention difference of that size. Noun-phrase elaboration counts the dependents of common nouns with the relations amod, nmod, acl, nummod or appos, leaving out determiners, whose rates alone differ twentyfold across treebanks. It replaces noun-phrase depth, which was the least stable feature under translation. Across PUD texts, depth's median correlation with English was .39, against .64 for elaboration, which agreed better in 11 of 13 languages, and the two correlated .86 to .91. Hebrew is parsed with IAHLTwiki, which is native annotation of contemporary text and marks the present tense, whereas HTB is news of the 1990s converted to the scheme. Portuguese uses Porttinari for Brazilian text, the variety served, and Bosque for European text. Traditional Chinese is parsed as served with each toolkit's Traditional GSD package. Native parsing proved about as reliable as conversion to Simplified script, at .836 against .825 on GSD and .746 against .765 on PUD, and both PUD routes are reported. In the 14 languages that have a second Stanza package, it runs on the fixed sample of 2,000 texts per language. Only its correlations are reported, and it is never averaged in, because it changes the annotation convention. Each language's correlation between subordination and clauses per sentence is reported with the per-language quality table, since it is already .97 to .98 on the hand-annotated Chinese PUD.

Other parsers were considered and rejected. Trankit's pretrained models [@nguyenTrankitLightweightTransformerbased2021] remain at release 2.5 of Universal Dependencies. COMBO beat Stanza in attachment score, the share of words whose grammatical relation to another word the parser gets right, in all seven treebanks it was tested on with hand-annotated tokenisation [@klimaszewskiCOMBOStateoftheartMorphosyntactic2021]. It takes tokenised input, however, and uses a different encoder in each language. With hand-annotated tokens, a fine-tuned large language model beat UDPipe 2 by 2.0 to 3.7 points on Arabic PADT and Simplified Chinese GSDSimp. On Hebrew HTB and Turkish IMST, which its fine-tuning left out, it scored 70.0 and 53.5 [@matsudaStepbystepInstructionsSimple2025], and such models parse poorly without fine-tuning [@ezquerroBetterBenchmarkingLLMs2025].

Connective inventories are induced from parallel text. One registered translation-spotting procedure induces every inventory [@laaliInducingDiscourseConnectives2014], counting co-occurrence only over aligned sentence pairs whose English side carries anchors of one relation class. The English anchors were chosen on the hand-annotated GUM corpus. The causal anchors are *because*, *therefore*, *thus* and clause-initial *so*, and the contrastive anchors are *but*, *however*, *although*, *though*, *even though*, *even if* and *whereas*. A target form joins a class only if it occurs in at least 20 pairs. The lower Wilson bound of the share of its pairs whose English side carries the class's anchor must also be at least .50, and its dominance over the other classes at least .80. Hygiene rules block pronouns, finite verbs, names, numerals and the expressions *and so on* and *not X but Y*. In Korean, the forms are the connective-ending morphemes of the Kaist treebank, which carry most causal links and half the contrastive ones. The primary inventory is induced after acceptance and before linkage from the catalogue's own aligned pairs on the fixed sample, so that genre and translator match the texts read. It needs 300 single-class English anchor sentences per class and fold, with the gate cross-fitted on two folds. Below that minimum, the aligned sample is enlarged by count alone to up to 10,000 versions, and failing that, the class uses the TED2020 inventory, drawn from human-translated TED talks. That inventory is induced by the same procedure before submission and deposited as forms and counts, as the benchmark and sensitivity inventory. On the eight public test sets with hand-annotated connectives, it came within 5 F1 points of the inventory read off the annotated corpus itself, or above it, in 10 to 12 of 14 comparisons. Its per-class F1, the harmonic mean of precision and recall, ran from 47 to 92. Those figures came from simpler tokenisers, so the registered rerun reports them again. <!-- PENDING: P52 --> TED's sentence-initial *So* leaked into 14 of its 18 inventories, so the inventory induced without *so* is a sensitivity analysis. From English into French and German, human translators gave up to 18 per cent of connectives no comparable form, against up to 8 per cent for machine translation [@meyerImplicitationDiscourseConnectives2013]. No detector trained on the shared-task corpora produces features. Their connective data cover 8 of the 19 languages, and the two strongest systems differed by about 22 F1 points on one test set [@braudDISRPT2025Shared2025]. With induced inventories, a syntactic filter cost recall, lowering Turkish causal F1 from 62 to 35, so it is a sensitivity analysis.

Dialogue spans are detected from the primary and alternate quotation pairs of release 47 of the Unicode Common Locale Data Repository, such as „…“, «…», »…«, 「…」 and 『…』. Any further marks that the structural counts admit are added. The direction of every ambiguous mark is read from its spacing. A line-initial dialogue dash opens a turn that runs to the end of the line, if line breaks survive within pages, and an opener unmatched at the end of its page closes there. In Hebrew, a straight double or single quotation mark is a gershayim or geresh only when letters stand on both sides, so detection runs on the stage-wide normalisation and never on lookup keys. Dialogue share is computed on the served text and on the English source, and the gates that decide which value a language uses are set out under Validation without human annotation.

Every per-language claim in @tbl-resources refers to the ten languages the structural sample showed: Dutch, English, French, German, Greek, Italian, Korean, Polish, Portuguese and Spanish. The app offers nine more, Arabic, Hebrew, Indonesian, Romanian, Russian, Simplified Chinese, Thai, Traditional Chinese and Turkish, and the extract may contain any of them. The same four rules apply to them, and @tbl-resources-more, after the paragraphs on Greek, gives their resources and the rules their scripts require. A language outside these 19 would be treated in the same way, with its resources reported before the feature inventory is frozen.

```{=latex}
\begingroup\small
```

| **Feature family** | **Primary resource, uniform across languages** | **Sensitivity resource, native where one exists** | **Coverage of the ten sampled languages** |
|---|---|---|---|
| Word frequency | Lists built for this study from the 2024 release of OpenSubtitles by one deposited script, described before this table [@tiedemannOpenSubtitles2024MassivelyParallel2026]. Mean log frequency, the rare-word share and contextual diversity come from the same pass | The same script run on the 2018 release. The SUBTLEX family, native per language. Contextual diversity in place of the mean-frequency anchor, in one refit | All ten for the primary. Each list holds 100 million lookup units, so the precision of the estimates is the same in every language. The 2018 release had 2,193 Korean files, against 60,040 in 2024, which hold about 178 million eojeols. Native norms exist for nine, eight of them peer-reviewed and the Italian one a conference release. Korean has no subtitle-based norm. Korean content words are looked up by morpheme, as described after this table, and the type and token counts behind each list are reported with the matched-token proportions. Four automatic gates check every list (Validation without human annotation). |
| Age of acquisition | Broad native rated sets, available for seven of the ten: English at about 30,000 words [@kupermanAgeofacquisitionRatings300002012], Dutch at about 30,000 [@brysbaertNormsAgeAcquisition2014], Spanish at 7,039 [@alonsoSubjectiveAgeofacquisitionNorms2015], Polish at about 4,900 [@imbirAffectiveNorms49002016], German at over 3,200, Italian at about 1,950 and Portuguese at about 1,750. French has a set restricted to 1,493 monosyllabic words [@ferrandAgeofacquisitionSubjectiveFrequency2008] | A resource predicted by MEmoLon's procedure [@buechelLearningEvaluatingEmotion2020], in a separate pooled sensitivity solution, for languages that meet the admission rule under Materials | Seven of ten on sets without a restriction on word length. Each native set is subject to the token-coverage rule, and the matched-token proportion decides each case. French has a second set restricted by word length, 1,225 words of one or two syllables [@lachaudCHACQFAMBaseDonnees2007]. The larger French set will be tested against the rule, although a list of monosyllables is not expected to pass it. For Greek, the ratings found cover 260 picture names [@dimitropoulouStandardizedSet2602009] and the 299 cross-linguistic words. No Korean set was found, so neither Greek nor Korean contributes age of acquisition. The cross-linguistic norms of Łuniewska and colleagues rate the same 299 words on one scale in 32 languages [@luniewskaRatingsAgeAcquisition2016; @luniewskaCrosslinguisticRatingsAge2019]. They are not used, because 299 words could not match 80 per cent of the content-word tokens of a story. Native-norm coverage was forecast on news and subtitles, so before submission it is re-measured with lemma lookups on the translated benchmark stories, which may admit native norms in more languages. The predicted resource could cover about 15 languages. Extrapolated norms carry error that is not psychologically inert [@hollisExtrapolatingHumanJudgments2017], and predictions carried across languages lost up to 20 per cent of their correlation with human ratings [@ljubesicPredictingConcretenessImageability2018], so they enter no confirmatory solution. <!-- PENDING: P50 --> |
| Surprisal | Goldfish, one GPT-2 model per language (`goldfish-models/<lang>_1000mb`, 124,770,816 parameters, 50,000-token SentencePiece vocabulary, 512-token window, 10 epochs), trained under one procedure on OSCAR 21.09 scaled by each language's byte premium (the bytes it needs, relative to English, for the same content) to 1,000 MB, under an Apache-2.0 licence [@changGoldfishMonolingualLanguage2026] | XGLM-4.5B (`facebook/xglm-4.5B`, 4.5 billion parameters, MIT licence), trained on 134 languages according to its model card, is the single-multilingual-model contrast in all 19 languages [@linFewshotLearningMultilingual2022]. Because it differs from the primary in multilinguality, scale, corpus, tokeniser and vocabulary at once, it shows how far the choice of resource can move the estimates without isolating any one cause. The controlled contrast is `goldfish-models/<lang>_100mb`, which keeps architecture, vocabulary, corpus and tokeniser fixed and varies the byte-scaled data tenfold | All ten at all four tiers, so coverage does not decide the tier. Only the 100 MB and 1 GB tiers share the identical 125-million-parameter architecture, the smaller two being 4-layer models of about 36 to 39 million parameters. The scaling equalises bytes, not training tokens. Byte premiums run from 1.000 for English to 1.293 for Korean and 1.967 for Greek, and in these ten languages, training tokens range from 210.8 to 251.4 million. Across all 18 models, they run from 186.8 million, in Turkish, to 251.4 million. On parallel FLORES-200 text, the Goldfish models' quality varies by a factor of 1.20 across languages, against 1.55 for XGLM-4.5B. The tier is also chosen on psychometric grounds. Surprisal predicts reading times through a linear link in 11 languages [@wilcoxTestingPredictionsSurprisal2023], and language-model quality tracked psychometric predictive power in 11 of 13 languages [@wilcoxLanguageModelQuality2023]. In eye-movement data from 10 languages, over XGLM models of 564 million to 4.5 billion parameters, surprisal from smaller models fitted early reading-time measures better than surprisal from the largest models [@devardaScalingCognitiveModelling2023]. For late measures, however, larger models held an advantage [@devardaScalingCognitiveModelling2023]. The same inverse scaling was replicated in Dutch, where GPT-2-based models predicted best overall and both effects varied with the evaluation corpus [@boeveSystematicEvaluationDutch2025]. Transformer surprisal fitted reading times best after about two billion training tokens [@ohTransformerbasedLanguageModel2023]. In the ten languages, the 1 GB models reach that level, at 2.11 to 2.51 billion tokens over 10 epochs. The Arabic, Hebrew and Turkish models fall just short of two billion, and the smaller tiers fall short of it. The developers state that Goldfish is built for cross-linguistic comparability and is not competitive with modern large models on high-resource languages. A contrast can tolerate XGLM-4.5B's poorer fit to early measures. The 10-language study above documents its behaviour on reading times, and the MECO check set out before this table extends that record to Dutch, Hebrew, both Chinese scripts and Brazilian Portuguese. If GPU time still runs short after the budget guard registered in the main text, EuroLLM-1.7B replaces the contrast, with mGPT for Hebrew, Indonesian and Thai. mGPT is not a primary choice, because its model card lists neither Dutch nor Chinese. |
| Word length, lexical density, lexical diversity | Computed from the text and its parse, so no norm is involved. Word length counts letters per content word, names excluded, by script. Latin, Greek and Cyrillic letters are counted without combining marks, and Arabic and Hebrew letters as base letters. Korean counts conjoining jamo after canonical decomposition, Chinese counts Han characters, and Thai counts consonants and vowels without tone marks. Lexical density is the share of words, in the outcome's unit, that contain a content syntactic word, with punctuation and names excluded. Diversity is the moving-average type-token ratio over 50 content lemmas [@covingtonCuttingGordianKnot2010], chosen over the Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity because it is the more stable of the two at the length of these stories | The mean length of all words. Diversity over windows of 25 and 100 lemmas, over content forms and over all words, and the Measure of Textual Lexical Diversity [@mccarthyMTLDVocdDHDD2010], with each version's per-language correlation with the primary reported | All ten. The window changes the values [@bestgenMeasuringLexicalDiversity2024], hence the reported variants. On the parallel PUD treebanks, diversity over content lemmas agreed with English at .55 to .78, against .01 to .62 over all words, because type-token ratios on word forms also track inflection [@kettunenCanTypetokenRatio2014]. The gain came from counting content words alone, and lemmatising added nothing distinguishable from zero, so diversity over content forms is a registered variant. In Korean, letters are the jamo of Hangul, as argued after this table. The Korean syllable-block count enters no component solution, and its correlation with the jamo count is reported with the feature-pipeline validation. |
| Concreteness | Native human ratings only, with no value predicted or projected | A resource predicted by MEmoLon's procedure, in a separate pooled sensitivity solution, for languages that meet the admission rule under Materials | Nine of ten, with sets of about 1,100 to 40,000 items [@brysbaertConcretenessRatings402014]. Korean is the one language with no usable set. Its only published concreteness ratings cover 450 nouns in an affective word list [@hongDevelopingKoreanAffect2016]. Its larger rated sets measure other constructs, imageability for 665 nouns [@parkInvestigationAssociationFrequency2004] and perceptual strength for 1,000 words [@leeCrosslinguisticComparisonPerceptual2023]. The latter's concreteness values were taken from English translations, so the second rule under Materials excludes them. Native concreteness is not computed for Korean. Greek is admitted on a set of 2,948 words rated for concreteness and imageability [@traikapiGreekCypriotWord2024], subject to the same token-coverage rule as every other language and to the caveats stated after the table. Even an admitted set of a few thousand items is unlikely to match 80 per cent of the content-word tokens of a story. Concreteness is expected to survive the token-coverage rule in English and Dutch and possibly in Polish and Portuguese, with the matched-token proportion deciding each case. The predicted resource could cover about 16 languages. <!-- PENDING: P50 --> Published predictions for 77 languages were validated in Dutch only [@thompsonAutomaticEstimationLexical2018]. |
| Dependency distance, clause structure and noun-phrase elaboration | The unweighted mean of Stanza [@qiStanzaPythonNatural2020] in its `nocharlm` tier and UDPipe 2 [@strakaUDPipe20Prototype2018], run as set out before this table. Each toolkit applies one architecture to the same treebank in every language, so the mean satisfies the uniformity rule (the first rule under Materials). Taking each language's most accurate package instead would fit a different pretrained encoder in each language, such as a Greek BERT for Greek and a Dutch RoBERTa for Dutch. Korean, for which Stanza has only `nocharlm` packages, would have no encoder-based counterpart at all. Such a choice would confound the method of measurement with the language, a confound the uniformity rule exists to prevent | Each parser alone. A second Stanza package, where the language has one, on the fixed sample, reported as correlations and never averaged in. Clause heads counted from each word's own label, as a descriptive analysis | All ten in both. One named single-treebank package is fixed per language, giving each language one annotation convention. The treebanks are Alpino for Dutch, GUM for English, GSD for French, HDT for German, GDT for Greek, ISDT for Italian, Kaist for Korean, PDB for Polish, Porttinari for Portuguese and AnCora for Spanish. Both parsers take the same sentences, each with its own tokeniser, so their disagreement measures tokenisation and parsing together and feeds the error model (Measurement error and calibration). Published attachment scores decide nothing. The maintainers' table for Stanza 1.5.1 on release 2.12 reports single-treebank packages with a character language model where one exists. It therefore gives `nocharlm` figures only for Greek, Korean, Romanian and Traditional Chinese, whose packages have none. Its scores run from 85.5 on Korean Kaist to 93.6 on German HDT in these ten languages. No accuracy is published for release 1.15.0, which tracks release 2.18, one release later than UDPipe 2's newest models. The `nocharlm` packages use the CoNLL 2017 word vectors except in Simplified Chinese and Thai. Counting clause heads from each word's own label was less valid against the registered composite computed from hand annotation in 12 of 28 hand-annotated sets, and its higher reliability came from redundancy with clauses per sentence. One limit is left unresolved: the five grammatical features are computable from universal-dependencies output in all ten languages but are not comparable in level across them. Standardising within language equates scale without changing what a token is or which relations exist, so a pooled grammatical coefficient averages ten differently calibrated measures. |
| Adjacent-sentence similarity | multilingual-E5-large-instruct [@wangMultilingualE5Text2024], identified by checkpoint, since no DOI is registered, and prompted with its developers' instruction for semantic similarity on both sentences of a pair. A massive multilingual benchmark found it the best-performing publicly available model, with only 560 million parameters [@enevoldsenMMTEBMassiveMultilingual2025], and on public parallel text it beat BGE-M3 in 22 of 24 sentence-level comparisons | BGE-M3 [@chenM3EmbeddingMultiLinguality2024], peer-reviewed and covering over 100 languages, retained as the sensitivity encoder | All ten in both, and the per-language correlation between the two estimates is reported with the feature-pipeline validation. BGE-M3 is presented by its authors for retrieval, a different objective from sentence similarity. LaBSE is not used, because it is optimised for retrieving translation pairs, a different objective again [@fengLanguageagnosticBERTSentence2022]. The measure descends from the propositional analysis of the construction-integration model, and its vector-space form recovered the comprehension effects of two coherence manipulations [@foltzMeasurementTextualCoherence1998]. A cosine indexes semantic relatedness between adjoining sentences. Because it rises with topical overlap whether or not the second sentence takes up a referent from the first, the measure is reported as relatedness, not coreference. Raw cosines differ in level between languages, but adjacent and random pairs separated in every language (AUC .946 to .982). Pairs also ranked alike across translations (*r* = .87 to .94), so standardising within language suffices. The choice of embedding model can change estimated effects of semantic association on reading times [@ostergaardModelingSemanticAssociation2026]. Before submission, the text-level agreement of the two encoders and Qwen3-Embedding-4B is therefore tabulated on the translated benchmark for description only. <!-- PENDING: P51 --> At the word level, the reading-time effect of semantic distance disappeared once surprisal was controlled [@frankWordEmbeddingDistance2017], and LexicalDifficulty contains surprisal. |
| Referential overlap | Computed from the parse, with no coreference resolver involved. For referential overlap as defined under Materials, a content lemma is in a nominal position when its universal part-of-speech tag is NOUN or PROPN, or X in Arabic, whose treebank tags names X | Anaphoric continuation, which also counts a pair as continuous when the next sentence's main clause has a third-person pronoun subject or, where the dropped-subject gate is passed, a dropped one. An overlap anchor masked by the English source's coreference chains, projected through the word aligner [@grishinaKnowledgeleanProjectionCoreference2015] | All ten. Of the variants tested, overlap changed least under translation (κ with English .58 to .88), and parser error moved it least. Coreference is resolved in no translation, because the multilingual coreference corpora cover 9 of the 19 languages [@novakFindingsFifthShared2026] and transfer to a language absent from training loses 17.9 points [@strakaCorPipeCRAC20262026]. CorPipe 26 [@strakaCorPipeCRAC20262026], with its umT5-xl one-stage model, instead resolves coreference on every English source as a validation reference. On the shared-task minitest of a fantasy-fiction corpus [@hanFantasyCorefCoreferenceResolution2021], it scores 79.3, against 75.1 for its mT5-large fallback [@strakaCorPipeCRAC20262026, Table 7]. Each language's κ between projected English chain continuity and its own overlap is reported beside the English-internal ceiling. A variant that adds pronouns to the tag set is not used, because dropped subject pronouns distort it. Diluted over a story, per-sentence savings of 5 to 25 per cent from overlap would move log time per word by 0.018 to 0.090 standard deviations per standard deviation of overlap. Those savings are an assumption, as Section S5 explains. |
| Causal and contrastive connective density | Connectives per 100 words of the outcome's unit, counting the cues a reader met in the version served, with the registered $\log(1 + x)$ rule. Untransformed, they form the cue term of the Hypothesis 3 decomposition under Confirmatory models. Each language's inventory is induced after acceptance and before linkage from the catalogue's own aligned pairs, by the procedure described before this table | The TED2020 inventory, induced by the same procedure before submission. The inventory induced without the English anchor *so*. A syntactic filter on candidate forms | All ten. A density's error is detection error, measured as precision and recall per relation class, English included. It is measured against public hand annotation where that exists [@braudDISRPT2025Shared2025] and elsewhere as projected from the English source on the fixed sample. Five of the ten (Dutch, French, Greek, Korean and Spanish) have no public hand-annotated connectives, so only the cross-lingual gate validates their inventories. A story's split-half reliability of connective use describes how evenly the story uses connectives. It is never used as an attenuation factor, because internal-consistency logic does not apply to indicators that define a construct [@bollenConventionalWisdomMeasurement1991]. In public children's stories, causal density loaded .57 on the discourse component over all stories but .16 within tertiles of sentence length. Once sentence length was partialled out, similarity and overlap still shared a dimension, whereas the connective densities shared almost nothing with them. Published lexicons and annotated corpora serve only as validation references, and no person checks or labels an inventory. Empirical-Bayes and per-clause rates are not used, because they discard real variation in the stimulus or import sentence length. |
| Valence and arousal | MEmoLon, induced for 91 languages from a single procedure, at over 100,000 entries per language [@buechelLearningEvaluatingEmotion2020] | Native rated norms, whose size differs by more than an order of magnitude across the ten: English about 14,000 [@warrinerNormsValenceArousal2013], Dutch about 24,000, Spanish about 14,000 [@stadthagen-gonzalezNormsValenceArousal2017], Polish about 4,900 [@imbirAffectiveNorms49002016], German about 2,900 [@voBerlinAffectiveWord2009], Italian about 1,100 [@montefineseAdaptationAffectiveNorms2014], Portuguese about 1,000 [@soaresAdaptationAffectiveNorms2012], French about 1,000 [@monnierAffectiveNormsFrench2014], Greek about 1,000 [@palogiannidiAffectiveLexiconCreation2016] and Korean 252 to 450 [@leeEmotionEvaluatorExpanding2022]. The Polish set is taken from the corrected data released with its 2021 corrigendum, which repaired the values of 193 words | All ten for the primary, though not at uniform quality. The source evaluates its predictions against native rated norms in 26 datasets across 12 languages, among them eight of these ten, all but French and Korean. Valence correlates with native ratings between about .75 and .94, and arousal between about .50 for Greek and .78 for German. The Greek criterion was the 1,034-word set, whose raters agreed less on arousal than on valence [@buechelLearningEvaluatingEmotion2020; @palogiannidiAffectiveLexiconCreation2016]. The correlations are best judged against the agreement between independent native norm sets in the same language. Such sets agree far more closely on valence than on arousal, so part of the arousal shortfall is criterion noise that no resource could remove. Coverage limits the native-norm sensitivity analysis, because a list of about a thousand content words cannot match 80 per cent of the tokens of a story of several hundred words. We therefore expect the native comparison to run in English, Dutch and Spanish, possibly in Polish, and not in the remaining six. The matched-token proportion reported per language decides where it runs. MEmoLon is admitted for a language when it covers at least 80 per cent of content tokens, as the third rule under Materials requires. Under the second rule, its document means across FLORES-200 must also agree with those of the English originals at *r* ≥ .70. Lookups try the language-aware lower case, the surface form and the lemma, then a script fallback. That fallback is the content word of the multi-word-token expansion in Arabic and Hebrew and the content morpheme in Korean. In Chinese and Thai, it is maximal matching against the lexicon, which lifts Thai coverage from .65 to .95. Rows equal to a language file's unknown-word default are dropped. Provisionally, agreement runs from .77 in Korean to .85 in Dutch, Indonesian, Portuguese and Spanish across 17 versions, with Thai at .73 using its fallback. Hebrew (.81) and Romanian (.84) are therefore admitted, with a statement that no rated set was found for them. <!-- PENDING: P58 --> |
| Dialogue share, a secondary covariate in every confirmatory model | The share of a text's words whose first letter lies inside direct speech, with spans detected from quotation marks and dialogue dashes by the rules given before this table | The English-source value, which replaces the served value in a language whose detector fails the dialogue gate (Validation without human annotation) | All ten. Direct speech is read differently from indirect speech [@yaoContextualModulationReading2011], and silently read direct speech evokes voice simulation in adults [@yaoSilentReadingDirect2011]. Measures in the main text sets out why adjusting for dialogue share opens no collider path. A narrativity composite of past tense, personal pronouns and direct speech is not used. Every text is a story, so such a composite barely varies along its intended dimension, and within stories its parts cancel. On 1,200 public stories written by a language model, its three parts had a Cronbach's alpha of about -1.0, because past tense falls as dialogue rises. Its tense and pronoun parts are also not computable identically across languages. The Korean and Arabic treebanks mark no tense, and neither Hebrew treebank marks finite verbs. The French treebank tags the auxiliary of the compound past as present, and possessives are pronouns in some treebanks and determiners in others. Dialogue share is a covariate throughout, enters no hypothesis and is excluded from the component solution under Outcome-blind dimension reduction. |
| Predicted spoken duration per word, for the Hypothesis 4 adjustment only | Predicted seconds, the rate per unit times the text's spoken units plus 0.55 s per sentence end and 0.20 s per clause mark, divided by the words and log-transformed. The units are eSpeak NG 1.52.0 phones, through phonemizer 3.4.0, at 0.08 s each in the 13 languages written in Latin, Greek or Cyrillic script. They are Hangul blocks in Korean (0.19 s), Han characters in Chinese (0.215 s), PyThaiNLP 5.4.0 dictionary syllables in Thai (0.27 s) and letters in Arabic and Hebrew (0.10 s) | The measured per-text audio duration, if the data controller supplies it. Materials states when it replaces the prediction and when it serves a sensitivity analysis restricted to the texts it covers | All ten, with the matched-token proportion reported per language as for every other measure. Hyphenation patterns mark where a line may break, which need not be a syllable boundary. In public read speech, phones predicted duration better than hyphenation in every language tested. Where letters were also compared, phones tied or won. The constants are conventions: within a language, rates from 0.067 to 0.100 s give *r* ≥ .987, and sentence pauses from 0.40 to 0.80 s give *r* ≥ .97. The covariate reproduced a neural text-to-speech system's durations at *R* = .956 to .979 in seven languages. In 4,680 stories written by a language model, word length and sentence length explained 75 per cent of its variance, and pauses 44 per cent, so it partly measures sentence density. Its correlation with each component is reported before any outcome is linked, and the components' variance inflation factors in the duration-adjusted refit are reported beside the duration's own. This quantity enters no confirmatory model and serves the registered duration-adjusted sensitivity contrast. |

: Uniform primary and native sensitivity resources for the text features. Concreteness and age of acquisition have no uniform resource admissible in the confirmatory solutions, so the primary column gives native norms for both (the exception to the first rule under Materials). A predicted resource enters only their sensitivity solutions. Outcome-blind dimension reduction sets out how each source enters the component solutions. {#tbl-resources tbl-colwidths="[11,24,18,47]"}
