Korean has the fewest resources of the ten languages in the structural sample, though several of the app's other languages have fewer (@tbl-resources-more). It lacks a native subtitle frequency norm and any coverage in the cross-linguistic age-of-acquisition set. Its only published concreteness ratings cover 450 nouns from an affective word list, some of them names of neutral objects [@hongDevelopingKoreanAffect2016]. Its four sets rated for valence and arousal hold 252 to 450 words each, mostly emotion terms [@leeEmotionEvaluatorExpanding2022], and imageability has been rated for 665 nouns [@parkInvestigationAssociationFrequency2004]. At these sizes, none of the sets is expected to meet the 80 per cent token-coverage rule. Korean does have a subtitle frequency list built for this study, a Goldfish model, both parsers, induced affect and a lexical decision megastudy of 30,930 words and nonwords [@yiKoreanLexiconProject2017], which supplies decision times, not rated norms. Through the uniform resources, it contributes to the lexical and grammatical components and to the affective predictors, but to no analysis that requires a native norm. Korean also determined the parser tier, since Stanza publishes only `nocharlm` packages for all three of its Korean treebanks (see the dependency row of @tbl-resources).

The eojeol convention under Measures needs a separate rule for lexical lookups. The eojeol is the right unit for the outcome's denominator and for the parser-derived grammatical features, since the Korean treebanks are tokenised on whitespace. For a frequency lookup, however, it is the wrong unit: a surface eojeol carries its particles, so most eojeol forms will be absent from any word list. For the lexical features that require a lookup, Korean text is segmented into morphemes with the analyser Kiwi (kiwipiepy 0.24.0, model 0.24.0), which also tokenises the subtitles behind the Korean frequency list. Content status is decided by morphology, because about one content eojeol in eight in the Kaist treebank is tagged as a conjunction. A Korean content word is an eojeol containing a content morpheme, that is, a general noun, verb, adjective, general adverb or root. A proper-noun morpheme marks a name. The lookup is performed on content morphemes, which the list can match. An eojeol's value is the mean Zipf of its content morphemes, with the list's size counted in eojeols, and the values are aggregated to the text mean. On a list built from the 2018 subtitles alone, Kiwi already covered the content morphemes of 98.7 per cent of FLORES-200 eojeols. Both matched-token proportions, at eojeol and at morpheme level, are reported before the features are frozen. Without this rule, Korean would be expected to fail the token-coverage rule for frequency and to contribute no lexical feature.

In Korean, mean sentence length, mean dependency distance and mean orthographic length all rest on the eojeol, a unit that bundles a content word with its grammatical particles [@baekReadingSpacedUnspaced2023]. For that reason, the Korean lexical slope is interpreted on its own, as Measures requires of every Korean association, and is not compared like for like with other languages' lexical slopes. Hangul is written in syllable blocks. Korean kindergarten children identified consonant-vowel blocks better than consonant and vowel letters, and their identification of these blocks predicted word reading over and above letter knowledge [@choSyllableLetterKnowledge2009]. Among 74 children from kindergarten to grade 3 reading isolated words aloud, naming latency rose with length in both jamo (letters) and blocks, less steeply in older children [@juInfluenceOrthographicUnits2022]. Once word frequency was modelled, neither count had a main effect. The jamo effect still declined with age, whereas the block effect varied with frequency but no longer reliably with age. Because the two counts were collinear, their effects were estimated in separate models. Among 94 university students, lexical decision latency did not differ significantly between two- and three-block words [@paeLexicalPropertiesInfluencing2020]. Every block in these words had a final consonant, so they also differed in jamo, six against nine. The null result therefore applies equally to both counts.

Neither length study separates the two counts, so the choice between them rests on comparability. The jamo count will be the Korean length measure because it is a letter count like those of the other languages, and the block count will enter only the correlation described in @tbl-resources. Jamo are counted after Unicode canonical decomposition, which treats a doubled or compound letter as one jamo and a silent initial ㅇ as one. This convention reproduces the ranges of letter length reported by @juInfluenceOrthographicUnits2022. Both length findings come from isolated words, and whether length drives the lexical component in Korean text remains open. Korean's congruence with the pooled component solution will therefore be reported whether or not Korean is among the five largest languages. Where Korean has fewer than the 100 distinct eligible texts required for a language-specific solution, the correlations of its features with the pooled component scores will be reported in place of its congruence.

Before submission, a registered search looks for further Korean norms, because a search of Crossref is a poor instrument for Korean-language psycholinguistics. Fixed queries are run in the Korea Citation Index and in RISS up to a stated date. They use the Korean terms for concreteness (구체성), imageability (심상성, 심상가), age of acquisition (습득연령), valence (정서가) and arousal (각성가). The hit lists are exported and deposited. Their abstracts are translated by the pinned open translation model that builds the translated benchmark and screened by size, so that a set qualifies only if it rates at least 1,000 words. A qualifying set then faces the token-coverage rule, and a set that passes enters the analyses that use a native norm for the same feature. We will also ask Tae and colleagues about the unpublished norming study behind the emotion ratings of their 1,544 words [@taeEmotionalArousalEffects2026]. <!-- PENDING: P56 -->

The classification of orthographic depth used in the main text [@seymourFoundationLiteracyAcquisition2003] omits Korean and Polish, so both are placed from other sources. The two placements are fixed with the feature inventory and will not be revised in the light of the per-language estimates. Two meta-analyses from one research group, both drawing on that classification, coded Korean as shallow for reading, and French and English as deep [@leeRelationsMorphologicalAwareness2023; @leachmanRelationTextReading2025]. The first coded Korean as deep for spelling, because Korean spelling preserves morphemes across resyllabification, which makes words harder to spell than to decode. The outcome here is reading time, so Korean will be annotated as shallow in the reading direction. Each meta-analysis coded depth as a dichotomy, so Korean will be placed shallower than French and English but not ranked among the seven sampled orthographies placed shallower than French, Polish included. Two further sources agree that Korean is shallower than English. The editors of a survey of seventeen orthographies give Finnish and Korean as examples of the most transparent alphabetic orthographies [@perfettiEpilogueUniversalsParticulars2017]. The Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus classes Korean as moderately transparent, beside Dutch and German [@siegelmanExpandingHorizonsCrosslinguistic2022]. A benchmark of grapheme-to-phoneme conversion instead calls Hangul relatively deep, because its spelling leaves sound changes across syllable boundaries unmarked [@gormanSIGMORPHON2020Shared2020].

In the judgement of @awramiukReadingSpellingAcquisition2013, Polish is less shallow than Italian or Finnish but less opaque than English or French. In grapheme-to-phoneme entropies computed over the same nouns in 16 languages, it lies between German and Portuguese, nearest Portuguese [@schuppertWriteYouSpeak2017]. The classification places German at the second level and Portuguese at the third. Polish will therefore be annotated at the middle level, beside Dutch and Portuguese. That placement is less secure than those taken from the classification itself. Polish is more consistent for reading than for spelling [@awramiukReadingSpellingAcquisition2013; @lockiewiczPhonologicalProcessingReading2017], and one study of Polish children, citing the same entropies, groups it with Finnish, German and Greek as a transparent orthography [@debskaReadingSpellingSkills2019]. One of the two meta-analyses codes Polish as deep, but only in an appendix table and without naming a source [@leachmanRelationTextReading2025].

The app's other alphabetic languages are placed on the principle applied to Korean, by their consistency in the reading direction. Indonesian is grouped with Finnish and Italian as an orthography in which a letter is almost always pronounced the same way whatever the word [@borleffsMeasuringOrthographicTransparency2017, p. 1620]. The Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus classes Turkish as transparent, beside Finnish, Greek, Italian and Spanish [@siegelmanExpandingHorizonsCrosslinguistic2022, Table 1]. No comparative measure we found includes Romanian, but a study of its early readers describes its orthography as rather transparent, with most sounds written by a single letter [@doleanLanguageSkillsNot2021]. Indonesian, Romanian and Turkish will therefore be annotated as shallow, the Romanian placement resting on the weakest evidence of the three. The same corpus classes Russian as moderately transparent, beside Dutch, German and Korean [@siegelmanExpandingHorizonsCrosslinguistic2022, Table 1]. Russian spelling is, however, asymmetric: highly consistent from spelling to sound and much less so from sound to spelling, because of vowel reduction and voicing assimilation [@rakhlinPhonemicAwarenessIs2014]. Like Korean, Russian will therefore be annotated as shallow in the reading direction.

Of the four languages the delivered story texts add, Bulgarian, Hungarian and Serbian will also be annotated as shallow. Hungarian, whose orthographic properties resemble those of Finnish, was grouped with it at the lowest of three levels of orthographic complexity [@landerlPredictorsDevelopmentalDyslexia2013]. Bulgarian is described as a transparent orthography with highly consistent grapheme-phoneme correspondences [@marziComparableReadingDevelopment2026], and a comparison of Bulgarian and Spanish children learning to read treats both languages as consistent orthographies [@lopezescribanoRapidAutomatizedNaming2018]. The second wave of the Multilingual Eye-movement Corpus classes Serbian as transparent, beside Spanish and Turkish [@siegelmanWave2Multilingual2025, Table 2]. In a comparison with English and Hebrew, Serbo-Croatian was the shallowest of the three orthographies [@frostStrategiesVisualWord1987]. No comparative measure we found includes Kazakh, nor did we find any study of children learning to read it. A speech-synthesis study notes that native Kazakh words are spelled much as they are pronounced, whereas the many loanwords from Russian usually keep their Russian spelling and pronunciation [@mussakhojayevaKazakhTTS2ExtendingOpenSource2022]. Kazakh's provisional annotation as shallow rests on that description alone, the weakest evidence behind any placement. The classification's five levels were built to order European alphabets, so Arabic, Hebrew, Thai and Chinese are not placed on them. Arabic and Hebrew are annotated as abjads, Thai as an abugida and Chinese, in both scripts, as morphosyllabic.

Greek is the next weakest in norms, though not in the suitability of its writing system. Its orthography is transparent enough for every word to be aligned completely between graphemes and phonemes, and that transparency has been quantified separately in the reading and the spelling direction [@protopapasComparativeQuantitativeAnalysis2009]. Greek children reach accurate foundation word reading within the first school year [@seymourFoundationLiteracyAcquisition2003]. Among 234 Greek children followed through the first two grades, word reading fluency predicted accuracy by the second grade, but no path from accuracy to fluency was found [@georgiouCrosslaggedRelationsWord2025]. Greek has two sets rated for valence and arousal, and neither is expected to meet the token-coverage rule for the native-norm affective sensitivity analysis. One covers 348 words, rated for valence, arousal and other dimensions by 229 native Greek speakers at the University of Cyprus [@vaiouliAffectivePsycholinguisticNorms2023]. The other covers the 1,034 words of the Affective Norms for English Words, translated into Greek and rated anew by 105 native Greek speakers [@palogiannidiAffectiveLexiconCreation2016]. For concreteness, Greek has a set of 2,948 words rated for concreteness and imageability, most of them nouns [@traikapiGreekCypriotWord2024]. The set is available only as a preprint, and its 312 concreteness raters were Greek-Cypriot adults. Both facts will be stated wherever a Greek concreteness value is reported.

The app's nine other languages are covered by the same uniform resources. The frequency lists are built for all 19, those for Chinese and Thai after segmentation with the frozen word segmenter. Goldfish publishes no 1 GB model for Traditional Chinese. For lookups and surprisal only, Traditional Chinese text is therefore converted to Simplified script with OpenCC 1.4.2 in its `tw2s` mode, never `tw2sp`, which replaces Taiwanese vocabulary. The variant characters 妳 and 牠 then map to 你 and 它, pairs that the 1955 list of variant characters records, so the conversion normalises variants and translates nothing. The result is looked up in the Simplified list, and a list built from the Traditional-script subtitles is a sensitivity resource. Goldfish's native Traditional-script model is a sensitivity analysis for surprisal. The parse and the sentence encoders run on the text as served. MEmoLon's Chinese values are not all in Simplified script, since about a third of its first 200,000 Han entries are Traditional forms. Its matched-token proportion is therefore reported on the converted and on the served text. XGLM-4.5B covers all nine [@linFewshotLearningMultilingual2022]. Stanza publishes `nocharlm` packages for each, and UDPipe 2 has models for each, Thai only in its latest release. Across all 19 languages, the attachment scores published for Stanza run from 64.1 on Turkish IMST to 93.6 on German HDT, with no Thai row. The byte premiums that scale each Goldfish training corpus run from 0.94 for Simplified Chinese to 2.74 for Thai.

Five rules for these scripts are registered with the inventory. First, as Measures sets out, a Chinese or Thai word is a token of the frozen word segmenter of the Stanza package fixed for the language, which segments the registered sentences before they are parsed. The same tokens serve the outcome's denominator, the frequency counts and every lookup, so a segmentation error moves all of them together. In Chinese, the segmenter runs on the continuous text, and its tokens are regrouped into sentences by character offset. Segmenting isolated sentences cost 2 points of word F1 and 4 of attachment score on GSDSimp. The same applies in any language whose benchmark shows a loss of word F1 above 0.5 points from isolating sentences. Second, Arabic and Hebrew write the article and some prepositions and conjunctions as prefixes to the word they precede. For lexical lookups in these languages, the parser's multi-word-token expansion splits each orthographic word, and the lookup is made on the content word. As under the morpheme rule for Korean, the value is aggregated back to the orthographic word and then to the text mean, and both matched-token proportions are reported. Third, a script that leaves short vowels unwritten does not show its syllables, so Arabic and Hebrew count letters for the predicted spoken duration. In public read speech, letter counts predicted duration better than the other units tested in both languages, so both join the duration-adjusted contrast for Hypothesis 4. Fourth, the union segmenter and the segmentation diagnostics recognise . ! ? … and their full-width forms as terminal marks, together with the Arabic question mark ؟. In Greek alone, the semicolon `;` is one too, since it is the question mark after NFC normalisation. Closing quotation marks after a terminal mark are skipped, and a colon never ends a sentence. Fifth, Serbian was delivered in Cyrillic, whereas both parsers' Serbian models are trained on the SET treebank, which is written in Latin script. Each Serbian text is therefore transliterated to Latin by the Serbian-Latin-BGN transform of release 47 of the Unicode Common Locale Data Repository, after NFC normalisation. The parse-based measures, the frequency lookups and connective induction run on the transliteration, and each token is mapped back to the served text by character offsets, so word counts stay those of the served text. The Serbian frequency lists are built from subtitles transliterated in the same way, so that files in either script count alike. The transform writes њ and нј alike as nj, but transliterating 39,689 machine-translated Serbian sentences of the translated benchmark to Latin and back changed 21 of their 342,980 tokens. Parsed in Cyrillic, the same sentences received the catch-all tag X for 70 per cent of Stanza's words, and the two parsers agreed on 13 per cent of labelled relations. Through the transliteration, Stanza tagged 0.01 per cent of words X, and the parsers agreed on 87 per cent. The NLLB translations gave 14 and 86 per cent.

Three further limits are recorded here. Thai's parse reliability on units the size of a translated sentence is untested, because the Thai treebank's 363 test units are defined by dependency. Stanza's Thai package also has no lemmatiser, so a Thai lemma is its surface form. Thai is nonetheless not excluded before acceptance. Its sentences come from the provider's per-sentence length arrays if the delivery carries them, and otherwise from the union segmenter. If the segmentation checks return every language to Segment any Text alone, Thai takes that route too. Before submission, both parsers are run on the Thai stories of the translated benchmark, and their disagreement and their shares of root, parataxis and conj relations are compared with the Thai treebank's. <!-- PENDING: P59 --> Thai takes the maximum domain factor (Measurement error and calibration), is flagged in every table, and is decided after acceptance by the floor of the sixth outcome-neutral check, like every other language. A refit without Thai is registered under Sensitivity analyses. Turkish expresses some connective relations with converbal suffixes, which a match on whole tokens cannot count, so Turkish connective densities cover free forms only. Finally, the stories in every language but English are machine translations of the English texts (Table 2 of the main text). A text property measured in a translation is a property of that translation, so the cross-language comparisons registered here compare translations of one set of stories, not texts written independently in each language.

Every affective value in this design descends from adult ratings. The induced resource is trained on adult English norms carried to the other languages by translation, and every native set named in @tbl-resources is adult-rated. The readers are children of 7 and over, and where child norms exist, the difference between child and adult ratings is age-graded across this study's two age bands. The overlap of valence and arousal with LexicalDifficulty, given under Measures, is one reason for entering them as main effects only, and adult rating is another. A covariate measured on an adult referent cannot separate a developmental change in reading from a developmental change in how a word is rated. For the languages in which a child-rated set is available, we will recompute mean valence and mean arousal from it at rating ages inside each band. Their correlations with the primary means and with each other will be reported, whatever they show, as a descriptive check that enters no model.

Several tools named in this section have no registered DOI, as is usual for research software distributed through model repositories. Such tools are identified by the checkpoint that the fourth rule under Materials freezes, and the identifiers are deposited with the feature-extraction code.

## Validation without human annotation

No step in validating the features uses a native speaker or any annotation made for this study, in English or in the 18 translated languages. Each check instead applies a rule fixed before submission to one of three references. The first is public hand-annotated text. It comprises the Universal Dependencies test sets, including the parallel PUD treebanks [@demarneffeUniversalDependencies2021], and discourse corpora annotated for connectives in eight of the languages [@braudDISRPT2025Shared2025]. Public fiction annotated for direct speech in English and German, and PUD's hand-annotated names, complete it. The second is the translated benchmark. Before submission, 2,000 public English children's stories [@eldanTinyStoriesHowSmall2023] are translated one sentence at a time into the 18 languages by MADLAD-400 [@kuduguntaMADLAD400MultilingualDocumentlevel2023]. Two hundred of them are also translated by NLLB-200 [@nllbteamScalingNeuralMachine2024], so the sentence boundaries of every translation are known. The professionally translated articles of FLORES-200 [@nllbteamScalingNeuralMachine2024] are a third benchmark condition. The third reference, after acceptance, is the English source of each served text. One registered sentence aligner [@thompsonVecalignImprovedSentence2019] pairs each translation with its source on the fixed sample of 2,000 story versions per language. It is admitted in a language only if its one-to-one precision on the translated benchmark reaches .95. <!-- PENDING: P41 --> Attachment accuracy against hand-checked parses is not used, because it needs annotators in every language and because correcting a parser's own output inflates its measured attachment score [@berzakAnchoringAgreementSyntactic2016]. @tbl-validation lists every check, its reference, when it runs and what it decides.

Projection cannot be scored against the boundaries it was built from, so the segmentation checks test what it assumes: translation sentence by sentence, accurate segmentation of the English source, and Thai renderings joined by spaces. Before submission, the union segmenter is scored in the three benchmark conditions by boundary F1 with 2,000 cluster-bootstrap replicates. A quotation mark placed on the other side of a boundary is not counted as an error, and exact matching is reported beside that score. The reference is the end of each rendering of an English sentence plus the translation's own sentence ends, found by a frozen rule that is conservative for abbreviations, ordinals and initials. Filtered English-Thai pairs from TED2020 add a larger human-translation condition for Thai. Each feature's segmentation noise is computed per language as an input to the error model, and the linearity of that noise is tested (Measurement error and calibration). Provisionally, the union segmenter scored 94.1 on FLORES-200 in Thai (95 per cent interval 91.8 to 96.0), against 85.6 for Segment any Text alone, 99.5 in Arabic and 97.9 to 99.8 in every other translation. In public stories translated sentence by sentence, it scored 94.3 in Thai and 97.6 in Arabic, against 80.8 and 83.0 for Segment any Text alone. In English, Segment any Text agreed with the frozen rule on all 382 boundaries of the benchmark. <!-- PENDING: P40 -->

After acceptance, the three segmentation checks registered under Outcome-neutral quality checks run on the fixed sample. The first, the merge rate, is measured in the languages where Segment any Text alone has a lower 95 per cent limit of at least .95 in both translated-story conditions, which the benchmark identifies. In those languages, the aligner pairs target sentences with English ones. Splits are only reported, since human translators split 1.8 to 10 per cent of English sentences. Provider sentence-length arrays, if delivered, serve as the exact reference. Two further reports are descriptive. One is the per-story maximum share of misplaced boundaries, because projection errors cascade within a story. The other checks whether each span lies closer to its own English sentence than to its neighbours under the registered sentence encoder.

Thai's accuracy rests on how the provider's system joins Thai renderings. Both benchmarks join them with a space, so every true boundary is a candidate. Without spaces, projection scored 79.9 (95 per cent interval 72.6 to 88.9) against the translated benchmark's known rendering boundaries. Only 24.9 per cent of its projected boundaries then fell at white space or a terminal mark, against 99.7 per cent in space-joined text. <!-- PENDING: P40 --> The third check therefore catches that case after acceptance. Before then, structural counts on the delivered translations, which involve no feature computation, can test a necessary condition: each Thai page needs at least as many whitespace runs as its English page has sentences, less one.

The connective gate and the dropped-subject gate are registered under Outcome-neutral quality checks. The dropped-subject rule of anaphoric continuation can apply only in the eight null-subject languages with agreement marking (Arabic, Greek, Italian, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Spanish and Turkish). Where its gate fails, only overt pronoun subjects count, and the language is flagged. The list of existential and impersonal predicates is derived mechanically from the treebanks' training data. Provisionally, Spanish passes on hand-annotated text (.830 and .938) and Turkish does not (.669 and .794). <!-- PENDING: P55 -->

Names are decided by a two-route rule, and no person reviews the inventory. Under the first route, a type is a name if Stanza tags at least half its occurrences PROPN, or X in Arabic. The second route projects the English source's names through word alignment with multilingual BERT [@jalilisabetSimAlignHighQuality2020], wherever the alignment covers at least half of the English names. Before submission, the exact rule is chosen from three candidates by the highest worst-case value, over the 18 translations, of mean F1 on invented names, on names that are also ordinary words and on real names. These are measured on benchmark stories with renamed characters and on PUD's hand-annotated names. The inventory is built after acceptance. In Arabic, name detection's precision is expected near .65, with recall of .87 to .88 on invented names. <!-- PENDING: P53 -->

A language keeps its own dialogue share if that share agrees with the English source's at *r* ≥ .80 across texts. Below that, it takes the English-source value, flagged in every table, which the rule on the English source under Materials allows for an adjustment covariate. The reported-speech rule for clause heads needs a sentence-level κ of at least .70 against the English source, and below that, a language takes speech status from the English source through the aligner. Before submission, the detector is validated on the public fiction annotated for direct speech and on FLORES-200 in all 18 translations, where the spacing rule provisionally lifts Arabic to *r* = .848 and κ = .772. <!-- PENDING: P54 -->

Four automatic gates check each frequency list in place of inspection. The script purity of its most frequent types must be at least .90. At least 80 per cent of the 50 most frequent closed-class forms in the language's Universal Dependencies test set must rank among the list's 2,000 most frequent types. At least 90 per cent of its 5,000 most frequent types must appear in an independent list, `wordfreq` or, for Thai, the Thai National Corpus [@aroonmanakunThaiNationalCorpus2009], with a rank correlation of at least .30. The list must also cover at least 93 per cent of the test set's content tokens. On the 2018 lists, every deliberately damaged control failed at least one gate. A list that fails leads first to a script fix applied to all 19 lists, then to the 2018 list, and only then to the loss of the frequency anchor in that language. The thresholds are frozen once all 19 lists are built.

A registered anomaly battery, set out under Outcome-neutral quality checks, replaces inspection of each language's texts. Its length-ratio check flags a ratio to the English source beyond three median absolute deviations. A feature that performs poorly in a language is declared missing there only if two conditions hold. An alternative tool must agree with the English source better than the primary one, by at least .10 with an interval above zero. The feature's noise-only $\rho^2$ against public hand-annotated text in that language must also be below .50, the floor that the sixth outcome-neutral check applies to components.

Every translated page is scored against its English source by MetricX-24-Hybrid-XL in its reference-free quality-estimation mode [@juraskaMetricX24GoogleSubmission2024], and a text's value is the word-weighted mean over its pages. In its developers' evaluation, this checkpoint averages .699 in that mode on the WMT24 meta-evaluation, against .712 for the larger XXL checkpoint [@googleresearchMetricX]. In the shared task, the quality-estimation submission built on the larger checkpoint scored .714 and CometKiwi .640 [@freitagAreLLMsBreaking2024], and CometKiwi's non-commercial licence also makes it the weaker choice. Before linkage, an outcome-free diagnostic reports, per language, the within-cell correlation of per-text disagreement between the parsers, and between the union segmenter and Segment any Text, with the quality estimate. Quality estimation is validated before submission in three steps. It is compared first with public WMT24 human judgements in the study's language pairs that have them, then with reference-based MetricX on the literary segments of WMT24++ in all 18 targets [@deutschWMT24ExpandingLanguage2025]. A screen of synthetic degradations comes last, because MetricX-24 was trained on such degradations. A metric that sees only the candidate translation scored .650 on WMT24 [@freitagAreLLMsBreaking2024; @perrellaGuardiansMachineTranslation2024], so the estimate partly measures target fluency, and with it part of the lexical predictor itself. The refits that use it are registered under Sensitivity analyses. <!-- PENDING: P57 -->

The three references catch failures that change counts or structure. Examples are missed or misplaced sentence boundaries, parses whose errors outweigh the variation between texts, inventories that do not follow the English connectives, quotation marks read in the wrong direction and names not excluded. Four limits remain. First, the noise is transported from hand-annotated text to the stories' genre, and the contrast nearest children's stories gave the largest domain factor, so several verdicts may prove sensitive to the calibration. Second, error that varies with translation quality is amplified by the correction, and the refits that use the quality estimate bound it without separating confounding from over-adjustment [@cinelliCrashCourseGood2024]. Third, errors in segmenting the English source are copied into every projected translation, so segmentation error is correlated across languages. Fourth, Thai's parse reliability on units the size of a translated sentence is untested, and its only hand-annotated text of that size, Thai PUD, gives a reliability of about .5 under a different convention. Some failures also pass unseen, such as a translation error that leaves a sentence fluent, a word that is correct but unusual for children, or a convention of children's writing particular to one language. A translation that legitimately restructures a sentence counts against its language, and agreement with the English source favours analyses that resemble English. Nine languages have no public hand-annotated connectives: Arabic, Dutch, French, Greek, Hebrew, Indonesian, Korean, Romanian and Spanish. Traditional Chinese has none in its own script. Every result is therefore reported as the pipeline's consistency with independent references, beside the slopes it qualifies.

## Measurement error and calibration

An unreliable predictor treated as exact inflates false claims of incremental validity, most of all in large samples [@westfallStatisticallyControllingConfounding2016], and noise does not always shrink estimates [@lokenMeasurementErrorReplication2017]. Excluding a language whose parse is less reliable would leave the attenuation untouched in every language that remains. It would also remove the languages most distant from English, whose parsers were least reliable on hand-annotated text and which matter most for any claim about reading beyond English [@shareAnglocentricitiesCurrentReading2008; @blasiOverrelianceEnglishHinders2022]. Regression calibration, by contrast, is unbiased for linear models when its parameters are consistently estimated [@keoghSTRATOSGuidanceDocument2020]. Prediction-powered inference and design-based supervised learning need hand-annotated labels sampled from the target texts [@angelopoulosPredictionpoweredInference2023; @egamiUsingImperfectSurrogates2023], which this design does without, and plugging predictions in unchanged biases regressions [@fongMachineLearningPredictions2021]. Simulation-extrapolation is asymptotically the method-of-moments estimator in linear models [@cookSimulationextrapolationEstimationParametric1994], and multiple imputation would need many full fits and the same transported calibration [@coleMultipleimputationMeasurementerrorCorrection2006]. The main text therefore registers calibrated component scores under Confirmatory models. This subsection sets out the error model and the constants behind them, and Section S5 reports the simulation that motivated the choice.

For each component and language, the reliability that governs the bias is the noise-only $\rho^2 = 1 - \sigma^2_U/\mathrm{Var}(W)$. Here $W$ is the score of the served text, $X$ the score the frozen pipeline would compute from correct sentence boundaries, words and grammatical structure, and $U$ the residual of $W$ on $X$. Under the linear measurement-error model, the attenuation of a within-language standardised slope is $\rho$, whatever the shrinkage $b$ of $W$ towards its mean [@keoghSTRATOSGuidanceDocument2020]. Parse error shrinks a score towards its mean and then adds noise, as survey reports of earnings do [@boundExtentMeasurementError1991]. The reliability ratio $R = 1 - \mathrm{Var}(W - X)/\mathrm{Var}(W)$ counts that shrinkage as error, since $R = \rho^2 - (1 - b)^2\,\mathrm{Var}(X)/\mathrm{Var}(W)$. It therefore lies below $\rho^2$ whenever the parse shrinks the score, as it does on hand-annotated text ($b$ = .787 to .953). Dividing a standardised slope by $R$ overcorrected by 3.6 to 28.2 per cent on hand-annotated text, mostly because it divides by a reliability instead of its square root. Parsers trained on a treebank share its annotators' systematic errors, and a reference with correlated errors can bias such estimates in either direction [@spiegelmanMeasurementErrorCorrection1997; @kipnisStructureDietaryMeasurement2003]. Reliability referenced to hand annotation is therefore not assumed to be conservative. For each language and component, $R$, the raw attenuation factor $\lambda$ and $\rho^2$ are reported side by side. On hand-annotated Universal Dependencies 2.18 text, the leave-one-out transport error of $\rho^2$ was .022, against .038 for $R$.

In the served texts, $\sigma^2_U = \gamma_U \kappa_U \mathrm{Var}_D$ plus segmentation noise. Here $\mathrm{Var}_D$ is the variance of the difference between the Stanza and UDPipe 2 scores within reading level, measured on every text the children read. The constant $\kappa_U$ converts that disagreement into noise for the two-parser mean. Its anchor-level error and disagreement covariances are frozen per treebank before submission, from 100,000 synthetic texts drawn with a registered seed under the long-unit rule for units over 100 words. They are evaluated at the frozen pooled weights after the catalogue fit. The unweighted $\kappa_U$ is primary, and an importance-weighted version is a sensitivity analysis [@ackermanCalibratingValidationSamples2021]. Thai's $\kappa_U$ comes from its treebank in a shuffled design and from Thai PUD. Kazakh has no $\kappa_U$, since it has one parser and too little hand-annotated text held out from that parser's training, so its components are treated as below the reliability floor (Outcome-neutral quality checks). The domain factor $\gamma_U$ carries $\kappa_U$ to the genre. It is the median over contrasts that hold the annotation convention fixed and can be identified by machine. These are the document identifiers of GUM, the written IAHLTwiki against the spoken IAHLTknesset, the document-identifier prefixes of GDT, and RRT only where its codes identify fiction without reading Romanian text. PUD contrasts mix convention with domain and enter only the maximum. Draws for propagation come from a log-normal fit to the contrasts. The leave-one-out extremes of $\gamma_U$ over the contrasts set the bounds of the calibration-sensitivity rule under Confirmatory models. No English stories are annotated for this study, so $\gamma_U$ rests on these contrasts alone. For the two-parser mean, the four contrasts give noise-only factors of 2.87 (GUM, written to narrative and spoken), 1.31 (IAHLTwiki to IAHLTknesset), 0.27 (GDT, written to transcribed speech) and 0.59 (RRT, other to fiction), so $\gamma_U$ is 0.95. Leaving one contrast out moves the median between 0.59 and 1.31, but the median of the other three misses a left-out contrast by up to a factor of 4.9, so the bounds are widened to 0.19 and 4.63. The log-normal fit has a mean of -0.13 and a standard deviation of 1.01 on the log scale, and the largest factor over all contrasts, PUD included, is 4.37. In machine translations of public children's stories, the parsers disagreed little enough that the slope correction for GrammaticalLoad would differ by about 4 to 27 per cent between the two bounds in 15 of 17 languages. In both Chinese scripts, the upper bound would take GrammaticalLoad below the reliability floor. <!-- PENDING: P43 --> Transport of a calibration from an external reference is an open research question [@liTransportabilityRegressionCalibration2026], and with only an external reference, sensitivity analysis is the standard safeguard [@shawSTRATOSGuidanceDocument2020; @siddiqueMeasurementErrorCorrection2019].

Each of the three components has an error model, computed from hand annotation and from the frozen pipeline on the same texts. The Universal Dependencies test sets and PUD serve for parsing and tokenisation, and the translated benchmark for sentence boundaries. Two error-prone covariates can bias each other in either direction [@rosnerCorrectionLogisticRegression1990], and learned proxies carry contamination from other concepts as well as noise [@knoxTestingCausalTheories2022]. The noise covariance $\Sigma_U$ therefore keeps its off-diagonal terms, and the cross-loadings $Q$ of each component's error on the others are estimated. Both are constants deposited before submission, and only the diagonal noise variances are rescaled to the served texts. Connective detection error enters where public hand-annotated connectives exist and is declared unmeasured elsewhere. Segmentation error is tested for linearity on the translated benchmark. Where adding the square of $X$ gains more than .01 of $\mathrm{Var}(W)$, the language's segmentation noise comes from the total residual, so the floor uses the larger noise. A language is flagged if its transported $\rho^2$ exceeds the method-of-triads value from the pairwise correlations of three parses of the fixed sample, by Stanza, UDPipe 2 and Stanza on a second treebank. Arabic, both Chinese scripts, Romanian and Thai have no second Stanza package, so there the flag is reported as not computable. On hand-annotated text, that value exceeded $\rho^2$ by .03 to .09, as it does when errors are positively correlated [@ockeBiochemicalMarkersAdditional1997; @mccollExtendedTripleCollocation2014; @luckeRasslingHogInfluence2005], so it bounds $\rho^2$ from above. Every constant named here is deposited before submission: the anchor-level inputs of $\kappa_U$, $\gamma_U$ with its bounds, $Q$ and the off-diagonal terms of $\Sigma_U$. <!-- PENDING: P42 -->

The floor of the sixth outcome-neutral check is a conditional $\rho^2$ of .50 within cell. Its unconditional equivalents are .600 at a variance inflation of 1.25 and .667 at 1.5, inside the range tested on hand-annotated text. There, with Stanza's parse and the noise-only domain factor of five contrasts (median 1.23, maximum 1.33), every condition tested provisionally passes at a variance inflation of 1.25. The lowest value is .551, for Turkish PUD. At 1.5, Simplified Chinese PUD sits at .510 and Turkish PUD fails at .461, and with the domain factor at its maximum, Simplified Chinese PUD falls to .469. Three of the five contrasts are PUD contrasts, which the registered rule admits only to the maximum. The forecast has not yet been recomputed for the two-parser mean, whose same-convention factors on total error exceed Stanza's, so these figures may be optimistic. The 19-language forecast for the two-parser mean replaces them before submission. <!-- PENDING: P44 --> A gate on $R$ at .80 would have failed 4 of the 10 conditions on hand-annotated text at a variance inflation of 1, although their standardised slopes were attenuated by only 11 to 20 per cent. @tbl-reliability gives the provisional reliability and segmentation accuracy of each language.

The main text's count of expected attrition is provisional until the 19-language benchmark has run, and the risks that benchmark will settle are these. Thai is decided as set out after @tbl-resources-more, with no imputation and no language-specific component set. Imputing systematically missing covariates needs many exchangeable clusters [@rescherigonMultipleImputationHandling2013; @audigierMultipleImputationMultilevel2018], and Thai is one typologically distinct language of 19. A lexical-only Thai slope would be adjusted for a different covariate set, so Thai can enter for its lexical component alone only through the partial inclusion registered under Confirmatory models. Arabic is provisional. Under the union segmenter, recall on its units without terminal punctuation rose from 55.2 to 97.7, but its error structure has not been measured on hand-annotated text. <!-- PENDING: P40 --> Simplified Chinese and Turkish are the tested languages at risk, and only in text resembling PUD at a variance inflation of 1.5. Traditional Chinese was not in the forecast, but its PUD reliability is slightly below Simplified Chinese's, so it probably shares that risk. <!-- PENDING: P44 --> Turkish is also expected to lose the dropped-subject rule. Hebrew stories rich in dialogue may resemble the spoken treebank more than the written one. The connective inventory induced on the catalogue may fall short of its minimum in some classes, which then use the TED2020 inventory. The restricted-weights check could also bind, since, on public stories, losing both connective densities left a restricted score correlating .947 with the full one, against .99 within tertiles of sentence length. That check and the Hypothesis 3 decomposition are both forecast on the translated benchmark before submission, and the forecasts are reported here. <!-- PENDING: P12 --> Dependency distance orders texts differently from English in Korean, Turkish, Chinese and German (*r* = .21, .29, .46 and .46 on PUD), so those slopes are read within language.

## The third parser

The third parser registered under Materials shares Stanza's architecture and uses the XLM-R-large encoder. It is admitted by rules frozen before any of its gains is computed, and any change made after the freeze to the code that applies them will be logged with its reason. The frozen rules and the parser's training recipe are deposited with this protocol, with their SHA-256 checksums. A pilot of its own decides first whether its full training goes ahead. That pilot trains it on Simplified Chinese GSDSimp and Turkish IMST and benchmarks it on their test sets and PUD. It gives a go only if it completes, two runs of the parser give byte-identical parses with as many sentences as the hand annotation and the projected cost of the full training is at most 150 L40S GPU-hours. The upper 95 per cent limit of the parser's gain, averaged over the Chinese and Turkish conditions, must also not be below zero. A criterion that cannot be evaluated gives no verdict unless another criterion fails. Every gain, in the pilot and after it, is computed with the version of the feature code that the frozen rules record, and only delivered languages count.

After a go, the third parser will be trained on the registered treebanks of the 18 delivered languages with hand-annotated text held out from every parser's training. It takes Stanza's tokens and multi-word tokens, so it adds no tokenisation error of its own. It adds its own tags, features and dependencies. Its lemmas come from Stanza's registered lemmatiser applied to those tags. The three-parser mean is unweighted, and a unit longer than 100 words takes Stanza's parse in every member of it, as in the two-parser mean. If the third parser joins, $\mathrm{Var}_D$ stays the variance of the difference between the Stanza and UDPipe 2 scores, and the three-parser $\kappa_U$ converts it into noise for the three-parser mean.

The joining decision will rest on the development sets of these treebanks, one condition per language, each parsed by Stanza, UDPipe 2 and the third parser. Kazakh is left out because it has no hand-annotated text held out from the parsers' training. A check on its hand-annotated text showed that Stanza's released Kazakh models were trained on the test file of KTB, and UDPipe 2 has no Kazakh model. The test sets and PUD take no part in the joining decision. If the third parser joins, its three-parser error-model constants are estimated on them alone. Constants estimated on the development sets would carry the selection that admitted it into the correction for measurement error, a form of the circular analysis that @kriegeskorteCircularAnalysisSystems2009 warn against. The pilot's go used the Turkish and Simplified Chinese test sets and PUD, but its gain criterion stops only a parser whose gain there is significantly negative, so the selection it carries into those constants is slight.

The decision assumes that the development sets are held out from the training of all three parsers. Stanza, and the third parser with it, trains on a treebank's training file and consults its development file only to select a checkpoint and to stop. UDPipe 2's models were trained with each treebank's original split into training, development and test files [@instituteofformalandappliedlinguisticsUDPipe2Models2025]. A registered held-out check will verify this before any development set is benchmarked. It will look up each sentence of a development set in each parser's training data by its sentence identifier, and by its text only where an identifier is missing. For Stanza, those data are the training files that its own data preparation makes from the registered UD 2.18 treebank, together with any training file of its released models that can be recovered. For UDPipe 2, they are the UD 2.17 training splits on which its models were trained. They are checked through the error model's record of which splits changed between releases 2.17 and 2.18, or against the UD 2.17 training files themselves where that record does not settle it. For the third parser, they are its own training files. A language whose development set overlaps the training data of any of the three parsers, or cannot be checked against them, will be excluded from the decision and will keep the two-parser mean. An overlap with the training data of Stanza or UDPipe 2 that the check failed to detect would flatter their parses of the development sets and shrink the third parser's gain. It would therefore bias the decision against admitting the parser.

The gain is the change in the noise-only $\rho^2$ of the five-anchor GrammaticalLoad composite on hand-annotated text when the third parser joins the two-parser mean. It is computed per language from 100,000 synthetic texts of at least 413 hand-annotated words, as in the error model, with the long-unit rule at 100 words. Its 2,000 paired cluster-bootstrap replicates use 10,000 synthetic texts each. Each replicate resamples documents, or blocks of 20 sentences in a file with fewer than ten documents, and scores all three parsers on the same resample. The two Chinese development sets hold the same sentences in two scripts, so they share their resamples. The frozen rules fix these numbers and each development set's seed. A development set counts as complete only if it was benchmarked from the hand-annotated file that the rules pin, with these values and its seed, and gave 2,000 finite replicates. A language is evaluable if its development set is complete and the held-out check shows it held out. The third parser joins if the 2.5th percentile of the replicate-wise mean gain over the evaluable languages exceeds .002, unless a veto applies. The mean weights the languages equally, because weights estimated from the same benchmark would add their own error [@claeskensForecastCombinationPuzzle2016] and would let the largest development sets decide.

The third parser is vetoed if its gain falls significantly below -.02 in any evaluable language. For each language, the one-sided bootstrap *p*-value for the hypothesis that the gain is at least -.02 is one plus the number of replicates at or above -.02, divided by 2,001. Holm's step-down procedure tests these hypotheses at a familywise level of .025 [@holmSimpleSequentiallyRejective1979], and a single rejection vetoes the parser. A veto therefore needs the smallest *p*-value to be at most .025 divided by the number of evaluable languages, the threshold at Holm's first step. With 18 languages, that allows at most one of a language's 2,000 replicates to lie at or above -.02.

The margin of .002 and the harm threshold of -.02 each set a smallest effect of interest against which the gain is tested [@lakensEquivalenceTestingPsychological2018]. The figures that support them are interim, and the thresholds will not move when those figures are updated. On the 15 test sets of delivered languages in the error model's interim benchmark, under the design the gain uses, adding UDPipe 2 to Stanza changed $\rho^2$ with standard errors of .0014 to .020 per file. Their root mean square was .0085, so an equal-weight mean over 18 languages with standard errors of that size has a standard error of about .002. A true mean gain of .009 then passes with a power of about .94, or .80 if the standard error is .0025. The margin absorbs the small advantage that the third parser takes from selecting its checkpoint on the development sets, an advantage diluted because it is one of three members of the mean. Stanza's released models also selected their checkpoints on these sets, but they enter both sides of the comparison. The same advantage makes the veto slightly more lenient on the development sets, and the gains on the test sets, reported beside them, decide nothing. <!-- PENDING: P46 -->

A loss of .02 is of the order of the gain that justified the second parser, whose mean gain in $\rho^2$ over Stanza alone was .027 on the same files. The veto is meant for losses significantly larger than .02. A loss three standard errors beyond -.02, about -.03 at the median interim standard error of .0038 and -.08 at the largest, is caught with a probability of about .44. <!-- PENDING: P46 --> Comparisons across many datasets call for a correction for multiplicity [@drorReplicabilityAnalysisNatural2017]. Whatever the dependence between languages, Holm's procedure keeps at or below .025 the chance of vetoing a parser whose loss is at most .02 in each language, up to the accuracy of the bootstrap *p*-values. An earlier draft of these rules, never frozen, vetoed the parser if the upper 95 per cent limit of its gain fell below zero in any delivered language. That veto would have stopped an exactly neutral parser, with a true gain of zero in each of 18 independent languages, in about 37 per cent of benchmarks.

The rule can be evaluated only once Turkish, both Chinese scripts and at least 15 of the 18 languages are evaluable. These three are required because the outlook under Outcome-neutral quality checks places Turkish and Simplified Chinese at risk, and Traditional Chinese probably with them, so a third parser could matter most there. A language whose benchmark is incomplete, or that the held-out check excludes, is reported and left out of the mean, the veto and the count towards 15. If the rule cannot be evaluated by the end point of the routes set out below, the third parser does not join. If the rule is met, the parser joins the mean only in the evaluable languages. Each other language keeps its registered parse, which is the two-parser mean, or Stanza alone where UDPipe 2 has no model, as in Kazakh. Once the full benchmark has run, whatever the joining decision, we will report each language's gain on its development set, on its test set and, where one exists, on its PUD treebank. We will also report the three parsers' pairwise error correlations. None of these reports decides anything.

After acceptance and before the deposit made before the extract is transferred, a floor guard acts when the reliability floor under Outcome-neutral quality checks is applied to the catalogue. The guard compares the conditional $\rho^2$ within cell that the floor uses. A language that receives the third parser keeps the two-parser mean if its GrammaticalLoad reliability with the three-parser mean would fall below the floor of .50 while the two-parser mean's stays at or above it. A language that falls below the floor with both means also returns to the two-parser mean. Only then does its Stanza parse fall back as registered under Materials, because no three-parser constants exist for a fallback parse. The floor reads the features of the served texts and the error model's constants and no outcome, so the guard is outcome-free. It cannot be computed from the benchmark, and it will be reported with the floor, together with the number of languages that the third parser moves across it.

Four routes, the preferred one and three fallbacks, keep this plan workable if the preferred route proves too slow or too costly. Each route is triggered by time, cost or the outcome-free rules above, never by a result that favours a hypothesis, and the rules apply unchanged on every route. On the first and preferred route, the pilot's verdict will be available by the checkpoint of 20 November 2026 and, after a go, the full training and the decision on the development sets by 27 November 2026. If the third parser joins, its constants from the test sets and PUD will be ready in time for the error model's final run. The second route applies if the pilot's verdict is not available by 20 November or the joining decision by 27 November. It also applies if the parser joins but its constants would miss the error model's final run before submission. A pilot without a verdict, like a joining rule that cannot yet be evaluated, counts as not available. The remaining steps will then follow after in-principle acceptance under the same frozen rules. The decision is computed on public hand-annotated text, so it cannot draw on the extract. The joining decision must be ready by the deposit of the frozen feature inventory, the component solution and the calibration inputs made before the extract is transferred. On any route, a parser that joins must also have its constants and its parses of the catalogue ready by then. If any of these is missing, the parser is declined, since nothing in that deposit is recomputed or deposited again after the transfer. The floor guard is therefore applied before the deposit too.

On the third route, after acceptance, the third parser's training under the second route and its parsing count against the budget guard of 400 L40S GPU-hours registered under Timeline in the main text. If the projected total exceeds 400, its parsing joins the guard's first step and runs with 16-bit (bf16) weights, provided its text means agree with those at full precision at $r \geq .995$ on the public benchmark. If the projection still exceeds 400 after every existing step of the guard, the third parser is declined. The decline comes after the replacement of XGLM-4.5B, because that model is a sensitivity contrast and the parser improves a primary feature. Every other step before it either keeps the parser, with bf16 parsing, or affects only models used for sensitivity or validation. On the fourth route, each language keeps its registered parse whenever the pilot gives a no-go, the joining rule is not met or the budget guard declines the parser. The same holds if the end point of the second route passes without the joining decision, as when the rule still cannot be evaluated, or without the constants and the catalogue parses of a parser that joins. The two-parser constants are deposited in every case, so the fourth route can be applied at any stage, and on every route the Stage 1 precision analysis rests on them. If the parser joins on the first route, the figures with its three-parser constants are reported beside them. That is conservative for reliability averaged over languages, since the parser joins only if it raises that average and no language shows a loss significantly beyond .02. It also stays valid if the parser is later declined or the floor guard returns a language to the two-parser mean.

# S4. The literature search

The Scopus counts reported in the Introduction come from three concept sets, each searched with one of the following expressions.

- Children's reading: `TITLE-ABS-KEY("reading comprehension" OR "text comprehension" OR "passage comprehension" OR "reading fluency" OR "reading time") AND TITLE-ABS-KEY(child OR children OR pupils OR "primary school" OR "elementary school")`
- Computational text features: `TITLE-ABS-KEY("word frequency" OR "lexical diversity" OR "syntactic complexity" OR "dependency distance" OR "text cohesion" OR "text coherence" OR readability OR surprisal OR "age of acquisition" OR concreteness) AND TITLE-ABS-KEY(computational OR corpus OR "natural language processing" OR "language model" OR psycholinguistic)`
- Platform log data: `TITLE-ABS-KEY("log data" OR logfile OR "log file" OR "trace data" OR "learning analytics" OR "app data" OR "mobile application" OR "digital platform" OR telemetry OR "behavioural logs" OR "behavioral logs")`

Each pairwise and three-way intersection reported in the Introduction joins the corresponding expressions with AND. All searches covered the publication years 2018 to 2026 in the field TITLE-ABS-KEY, with no document-type, language or subject-area limit. They were run on 26 August 2026 with scopusflow 0.4.0, and only count queries were issued, one request per count, so nothing was downloaded and no record set was assembled. The full record, including the yearly counts, is in `literature/scopus_search_record.md`. @fig-trends uses those counts to show how three related topics changed over the same years.

![Publication trend, 2018 to 2026, for children's reading comprehension combined with narration, with reading apps and e-books, and with machine-generated text, as a percentage of the reference set. The reference set is a query narrower than the children's reading concept set counted in the main text. Its expression is in `literature/scopus_gap_analysis.R` and its yearly counts in `literature/scopus_search_record.md`. The 2026 point covers only records indexed up to the search date of 26 August 2026. Shaded bands are 95 per cent Wilson score intervals on each yearly share. Because the counts are a census of indexed records, the bands illustrate how stable each share is, not its sampling uncertainty, and widen where the yearly reference count is small. Machine-generated text does not appear in this literature before 2024.](literature/scopus_topic_trends.pdf){#fig-trends width=90%}

## Reviews of reading on screen and of narration

@fig-evidence sets out the pooled estimates and review conclusions closest to two conditions of this study's setting, reading paged text on a touchscreen and narration that a family can switch on or off. Its sources were identified by a targeted search, separate from the accompanying systematic review. The search was run in October 2026 and extended in November 2026 to syntheses published from 2023 onwards. Where syntheses overlap, the figure keeps any that is the most recent on its comparison or that reports an estimate for children. It leaves out subgroup estimates that rest on fewer than four comparisons or that could not be checked against a full text of the source. For each value, `literature/evidence_map.csv` records where in its source it was found and which copy of the source was checked. In every row, the outcome is comprehension, on which this study's confirmatory results will say nothing. The figure therefore informs no registered decision and bears only on the constraints on generality stated in the Introduction and on the rationale for Hypothesis 4.

# S5. The design analysis in full

The precision analysis simulated data from the design specifications deposited in `design_analysis/`, and `design_analysis/run_design_analysis.R` reproduces it [@bernabeuPilotr2026]. The main text describes the three simulated models and what their omissions imply, and this section records how they were fitted and how the requirements were derived. Tier 1 holds the first eligible reading of each text by each account, and tier 2 the accounts with at least three eligible readings of distinct texts. The tier-1 and narration models were fitted by restricted maximum likelihood with lme4, with its derivative-based convergence checks switched off. Each simulated tier-2 child read five distinct texts in a random order, one at each session position. The accumulated-reading contrast has a standard deviation of one across the five positions, so its coefficient is on the per-standard-deviation unit that Hypothesis 6 registers. In the texts sweeps, each simulated reader drew one text at random, so twelve readings per text is an average and individual texts received more or fewer. In the three reading-time specifications, the child, text and residual variances sum to 0.998, and the effects that each sweep sets add 0.03 to 0.04. The simulated outcome's standard deviation is therefore 1.01 to 1.02. Relative to it, the effect of 0.10 and the bound of the region of practical equivalence, the range of effects treated as negligible, are 1 to 2 per cent smaller than their nominal values. The simulation thus set a slightly stricter test than the registered criterion, and its requirements err towards more texts and children.

Each requirement comes from a probit regression of the decision probability on the square root of the swept quantity, with each grid point weighted by its replicate count. The fitted curve is inverted at the target, and the delta method gives the requirement's 95 per cent interval. Where the two-parameter curve fits the grid worse than its replicate counts imply, the interval is widened by Pearson's heterogeneity factor. A target that the simulated range does not reach is reported as not reached, and the fitted curve is never extrapolated. The texts and narration sweeps used 200 replicates per grid point, and the readings, null and tier-2 sweeps used 120. At two readings per text, 4 of the 120 fits for each coefficient were singular and were retained in the widths and probabilities. The pooled grid in `design_analysis/precision_sweep.csv` gives, for each grid point, the Monte Carlo standard error on each decision probability, the number of fits attempted and how many converged, were singular or raised warnings. @fig-precision-sup shows the narration and within-child curves that the main text summarises.

![Precision for the narration contrast (a) and the within-child accumulated-reading term (b). Points are the probability of a determinate verdict for an effect of 0.10 standard deviations, over 200 simulation replicates per grid point in a and 120 in b. A verdict is determinate when its 95 per cent interval lies wholly outside the region of practical equivalence. Panel a assumes an average of twelve readings per text, and panel b five distinct texts per child. Shaded bands are 95 per cent Wilson score intervals on each probability, and the dashed line marks the 0.90 target. The narration curve assumes a balanced contrast, and the first adjustment to the main text's precision thresholds corrects its requirement by the design effect for the observed narration prevalence.](figures/fig_precision_supplement.pdf){#fig-precision-sup width=100%}

For comparison with Nature Human Behaviour's a priori power floor of 0.95 for frequentist plans, `design_analysis/solve_at_095.R` recomputes the requirements at that level from the same archived curves, without re-simulating, and writes them to `minimum_texts_095.csv`. At that target, the main effects need 926 distinct texts for lexical difficulty (95 per cent interval 794 to 1,069), 812 for grammatical load (723 to 906) and 784 for referential continuity (696 to 877). The grammatical-load interaction with the age band needs 1,510 texts (1,349 to 1,680), the narration interaction 1,506 (1,349 to 1,672) and the within-child term 731 children in tier 2 (621 to 851). The continuity interaction did not reach 0.95 within the 1,600 texts simulated.

For the Bayes-factor criterion registered under Decision rules, the requirements were computed from the same archived curves by `design_analysis/solve_at_bf10.R`, again without re-simulating. The reference prior is a Student *t* with 3 degrees of freedom, centred at zero, with scale 0.5 for a main effect and 0.25 for an interaction. Under it, the prior mass inside the region of practical equivalence is 7.3 per cent for a main effect and 14.6 per cent for an interaction. A Bayes factor of 10 for the region outside is therefore reached when the posterior mass inside falls to 0.8 and 1.7 per cent. For a normal posterior, those masses place the estimate 2.42 and 2.13 standard errors beyond the region's edge. The normal approximation is applied at each grid point. The mean interval width gives the standard error, and the probability that a true effect of 0.10 clears that distance is the normal tail beyond it. The resulting curve is inverted at 0.90 and 0.95 as in `solve_at_095.R`, and the requirements are written to `minimum_texts_bf10.csv`.

The approximation is checked against the simulation at the simulation's own criterion. At every grid point, the approximated probability of an interval wholly outside the region lies within 0.06 of the simulated one (`sweeps/bf10_calibration.csv`). Applied at that criterion, the same approximation puts the 0.90 requirement at about 715 texts for each main effect, against the simulated 738, 660 and 634, whose spread is Monte Carlo variation. Relative to the simulation's criterion, the Bayes-factor criterion raises the requirement by a factor of about 1.3 for a main effect and for the tier-2 term, and by about 1.1 for an interaction. The Bayes-factor requirements are reported under Design and precision analysis and in Table 1 of the main text.

The variance shares in the design specifications are assumptions, as Design and precision analysis states, so `design_analysis/run_variance_sensitivity.R` re-derives the tier-1 requirements with the share of variance between texts at 5, 13 and 20 per cent. The script holds the child variance at the specifications' value and the total variance at one, so the residual absorbs each change. It re-runs the texts sweeps for Hypotheses 1 to 4 with 200 replicates per grid point and solves each curve as the main analysis does, under the simulation's criterion and the Bayes-factor criterion, at 0.90 and 0.95. The rows at 9 per cent are read from the main analysis's cached sweeps and reproduce its figures. The 20 per cent sweeps were run on the University of Oxford's Advanced Research Computing cluster with the package versions of the main analysis. A re-run there of both 5 per cent sweeps reproduced the local results in every replicate decision, with mean interval widths agreeing to within $10^{-9}$. The results are in `design_analysis/variance_sensitivity.csv`, and the software versions in `session_info_variance_sensitivity.txt` and `session_info_variance_sensitivity_arc.txt`.

At 0.90 under the simulation's criterion, the three main effects needed 489 to 553 distinct texts at a text share of 5 per cent, 634 to 738 at the registered 9 per cent, 753 to 946 at 13 per cent and 1,146 to 1,243 at 20 per cent. Under the Bayes-factor criterion, they needed about 720, 930, 1,140 and 1,490, and at 20 per cent none reached 0.95 within the 1,600 texts simulated. A main effect is identified between texts, so its requirement rises with the variance between them. The two age-band interactions and the narration interaction moved the other way, and by less. At 0.90, they needed 1,256, 1,498 and 1,276 texts at 5 per cent and 1,141, 1,224 and 1,145 at 20 per cent. An interaction with a reader attribute compares readings of the same texts, from which the text intercept cancels, and with the total held at one, a larger text share leaves less variance within texts. The text share can be estimated only from a fitted model, so it enters none of the registered adjustments. Its estimate, the Text-level intraclass correlation reported under Measures, will show where on this range the extract lies.

The ordinal outcome of Hypothesis 5 was simulated and fitted with a separate script, `design_analysis/run_ordinal_analysis.R`, because the routine used for the reading-time models cannot fit a cumulative logit. Treating the three-category rating as continuous would avoid that problem but answer a different question. The script generates the rating from the same design specification, with each replicate seeded deterministically from its grid point and replicate index. On the latent logistic scale, whose residual variance is fixed at $\pi^2/3$, the specification's standard deviations give the text intercept about 2.5 per cent of the latent variance and the child intercept about 5.7 per cent, so the shares of 9 and 20 per cent stated in the main text describe the reading-time models only. The two thresholds, at -0.85 and 0.85 on that scale, are a placeholder that puts roughly 30, 40 and 30 per cent of ratings in the three categories, and the fourth adjustment in the main text replaces them with the observed proportions. It keeps each reading's rating with probability 0.30, the availability that the structural sample showed, and applies the protocol's five-rater floor inside every replicate. The model fitted with `ordinal::clmm` is a cumulative-logit counterpart of the registered model, containing only the three components, the age band and a text intercept. On the log-odds scale, the region is symmetric about zero, with the half-width of log(1.05) that the main text registers. Only a determinate verdict in the direction of the true effect counts as a success. The ordinal sweep used 60 replicates per grid point. In 14, 8, 4 and 1 of them at 200, 400, 800 and 1,600 texts, the text variance was estimated at zero and the standard errors were undefined. Those replicates are not a random subset, so none was discarded. Each was refitted as the fixed-effects cumulative logit to which the mixed model reduces at that boundary.

The rating sets the most demanding requirement in the design. At 200, 400, 800 and 1,600 generated texts, with an average of twelve readings each, the 95 per cent interval on a coefficient whose true value is 0.10 log odds has a mean width of 0.42 to 0.44, 0.30, 0.21 and 0.15. The probability of a determinate verdict does not exceed 0.30 at any grid point, so the 0.90 target is not reached within the range simulated, and no requirement is obtained by inverting the curve. The grid does, however, establish how interval width scales with the number of texts, with fitted exponents between -0.505 and -0.524 against a theoretical -0.5. A requirement projected from that scaling must also allow for attenuation, because the simulation generates child variance that the fitted model omits. In a logit model, that omission shrinks every coefficient towards zero, by a factor of about 0.967 at the specification's child standard deviation of 0.45 [@zegerModelsLongitudinalData1988]. The mean fitted estimates across the grid, 0.093 to 0.095 in absolute value with Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.004, agree with that factor. A determinate verdict must then clear the region's boundary starting from the attenuated value of 0.097, and doing so requires a mean interval width of 0.058. On the fitted scaling law, that width is reached at roughly 9,300 to 10,300 generated texts, of which about 2,700 to 3,000 have at least five ratings. Without the attenuation, the projection would be 8,200 to 9,000. Against the 634 to 738 texts that the three components need on reading time at the same criterion and target, the rating demands an order of magnitude more. The difference follows from a three-category response observed for 30 per cent of readings. These projections depend on the rating's availability across the full window and on how heavily texts are reused, which the provider-computed counts will supply. Before any outcome model is fitted, the simulation will be re-run at the observed values of both and at the category proportions observed in the extract. Those proportions matter because they fix the spacing of the simulated thresholds and with it the information a cumulative logit can recover. Design and precision analysis registers the re-runs at the observed availability and proportions as its third and fourth adjustments. Every number in this paragraph is reproduced by `design_analysis/summarise_ordinal.R`, which pools the stored grid-point results.

The simulated models also omit measurement error in the components and the variation of slopes across languages, and both raise the requirements. Attenuation by parse error inflates the variance of a corrected coefficient by $1/\rho^2$. With slopes that vary by language with standard deviation $\tau$, the posterior standard deviation of the population mean of the slopes cannot fall much below $\tau/\sqrt{L}$, where $L$ is the number of contributing languages. With few upper-level units, cross-level estimates degrade, and Bayesian estimation holds up better [@stegmuellerHowManyCountries2013], while standard errors at the upper level are biased with 50 or fewer groups [@maasSufficientSampleSizes2005]. The eighth adjustment under Design and precision analysis combines both with the variance inflation of the tier-1 design matrix, which scales the sampling variance [@obrienCautionRegardingRules2007]. Its form is $N = N_0 \times \mathrm{VIF} \times \overline{1/\rho^2} \times SE_*^2/(SE_*^2 - \tau^2/L)$. It comes from a two-stage normal approximation calibrated to reproduce the 930 texts that the Bayes-factor criterion requires of a main effect, which fixes $SE_*$ at 0.0135. Here $\overline{1/\rho^2}$ is the mean of $1/\rho^2$ over contributing languages. A two-stage simplification matches the one-stage model only where their assumptions match [@burkeMetaanalysisUsingIndividual2017]. The verdict quantity registered under Confirmatory models, the average slope over the analysed languages, has no $\tau^2/L$ floor, so the $\tau$ term applies only to the population mean reported beside it. In the planning calculation, the average's posterior standard deviation was .0139 with 13 languages, against .016 to .020 for the population mean at $\tau$ = .03 to .05. @tbl-tau gives the requirement for a main effect by $\tau$ and by the set of languages.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 19, error-free | 930 | 1,051 | 1,256 | 1,727 | 3,335 |
| 19, corrected | 1,132 | 1,279 | 1,529 | 2,102 | 4,059 |

It also assumes planning values of $\rho^2$ for GrammaticalLoad of .93 in English and .90 in most languages. The final table is computed at the deposited constants and the provider-computed counts, which will show how texts are spread over languages. Because translations of one story share a story intercept, it is reported in stories as well as in texts. The variance inflation is computed on the catalogue and on the tier-1 design matrix, as that adjustment specifies. <!-- PENDING: P60 --> The Hypothesis 2, Hypothesis 3 and narration interactions have no language-varying slopes in the primary model. If their slopes do vary, their intervals are anti-conservative [@barrRandomEffectsStructure2013], and the registered refit with language-varying interactions bounds that assumption.

A simulation of the pooled model motivated the correction. It generated 400 texts in each of 19 languages, with GrammaticalLoad measured under the error structure found on hand-annotated text, over 500 replicates. @tbl-inclusion-sim gives the bias of the GrammaticalLoad main effect and of its interaction with the age band, whose true values were 0.1008 and 0.10, and the coverage of the interaction's interval. The simulated gate removed Thai and every language whose estimated $R$ fell below .80. At 100 texts per language, the probability of a non-negligible GrammaticalLoad verdict was .694 under the gate, .760 corrected and .782 uncorrected, so the correction's gain lies in bias and coverage. No procedure gave a non-negligible verdict under the null. These results are provisional until the registered re-run described below. <!-- PENDING: P09 -->
