In provisional stress tests of 80 replicates each, effects at the region's edge gave the corrected procedure false non-negligible rates of at most .013 when reliability was estimated without bias. With heterogeneous calibration error and reliability underestimated by 15 per cent of the noise share, its rate for GrammaticalLoad was .050, against .062 for an oracle that knew the true reliability. With reliability underestimated by 30 per cent of each language's noise share, its rate was .062, against .025 for the oracle. <!-- PENDING: P61 --> An omitted cause correlated .3 with the parse noise biased the corrected slope by +6.4 per cent, against +0.3 per cent uncorrected and +0.7 per cent gated. A cross-loading of 0.10 of GrammaticalLoad's error on LexicalDifficulty, left out of the calibration, biased LexicalDifficulty by -0.0125, with coverage .766, against -0.0008 when it was modelled. At a cross-loading of 0.04, the bias was -0.0051, with coverage .976. Correction thus amplifies differential error, which is why the translation-quality refits are registered.

The simulation of the pooled model departed from the registered procedure in ways that favour the correction. It applied the floor to unconditional reliability and drew calibrations with equal variance in every language. It also assumed exactly linear, non-differential error and an unbiased cross-loading, and outside the stress tests it estimated reliability without bias. Before submission, the simulation is therefore re-run with four registered scenarios. The first applies the floor to conditional $\rho^2$ within cell, as registered. The second draws calibrations in proportion to each language's noise share, as drawing $\gamma_U$, $\kappa_U$ and $\mathrm{Var}_D$ implies. The third makes the error differential, with an omitted cause correlated .3 with the parse noise and cross-loadings of 0.04 and 0.10. The fourth misestimates reliability, under- and overstating each language's noise share by 15 and 30 per cent. Each scenario reports bias, interval coverage, the probability of a non-negligible verdict and the false non-negligible rate at the region's edge. It also counts the verdicts that the calibration-sensitivity rule leaves not conclusive. The scripts and their outputs are deposited with the other design-analysis files. <!-- PENDING: P61 -->

The effect of 0.10 standard deviations that every sweep assumed is a registered convention applied to every component, and for the connective densities the expected effect is far smaller. In 8- and 10-year-olds, an appropriate connective cut reading time by 7.5 per cent on its first clause and by 7.4 per cent on its second [@cainInfluenceConnectivesYoung2011, Table 4]. The control split the two clauses into separate sentences. The authors suggest that the first-clause saving may reflect sentence wrap-up, so with sentence length in the model, the connective-specific saving is about 7.4 per cent, on the second clause only. Diluted over a whole story, one standard deviation of cue density should then move log time per word by about 0.005 to 0.01 standard deviations, and nearer 0.005 to 0.006 on the second-clause saving alone. That study also found no age interaction during reading, which is direct prior evidence that the connective-by-age term is near zero. The same dilution applied to referential overlap, at assumed per-sentence savings of 5 to 25 per cent, gives 0.018 to 0.090 standard deviations per standard deviation, below the 0.10 assumed for the continuity component. That value is therefore an assumption that no source verified here supports, and the continuity requirements hold only if the component's effect is at least that large. Where the prior-derivation pipeline's pooled estimate lies between the region's half-width and 0.10, the sixth adjustment under Design and precision analysis re-simulates at that value.

# S6. Deriving the priors from the systematic review

The main text states under Priors which coefficients receive review-derived priors, when the rules of the prior-derivation pipeline were frozen and when the pipeline will be run. The rules are deposited verbatim as `priors/prior_derivation.md`, and the README of the `preregistration` directory records the revision copied and the copy's SHA-256 checksum. They were preceded in June 2026 by test extractions from 12 papers, made under an earlier schema and later used to refine the extraction instructions. An automated listing of the statistics reported in the included papers began in the same month. Here we summarise the fixed assignment of the review's extracted effects to this protocol's coefficients, the metric families and the pooling and de-duplication rules. LexicalDifficulty pools the review's word-frequency, lexical-coverage, other-lexical and lexical-diversity effects on reading. Before pooling, these are sign-harmonised so that frequency and coverage are reversed to the direction of difficulty, whereas age of acquisition, word length and surprisal keep their sign. Age-of-acquisition effects remain in the pool, and so partly shape the prior's centre, because the confirmatory component omits that feature only for want of norms comparable across languages. GrammaticalLoad pools syntactic-complexity and sentence-length effects. ReferentialContinuity pools coherence effects. The rules assign no review evidence to any secondary predictor, so the effects of discourse structure and of emotionality that the review extracts inform no prior here.

Pooling keeps metric families apart, because a conversion that is mathematically available is not always a valid one. The primary prior for a coefficient uses only standardised regression coefficients reported on the mapped predictor and outcome. No other metric is admitted to reach the two papers that the main text requires for a derived prior. Correlations, partial correlations recovered from *t* or from one-degree-of-freedom *F* statistics, standardised mean differences and odds ratios form separately named sensitivity pools, and no generic conversion from an odds ratio or a *d* to a correlation is applied to a continuous predictor. Estimates are pooled within an outcome class and never across classes, so a reading-time coefficient draws only on reading-time evidence and the rating coefficient only on rated difficulty. Unstandardised coefficients without convertible scaling, and rows whose direction the extraction could not resolve, are listed with the reason for their exclusion.

Within each combination of coefficient, outcome class and metric family, a random-effects meta-analysis fitted by restricted maximum likelihood pools one estimate per paper per relation, the one the extraction marks as primary, with the paper as the cluster. Labelled subgroups and alternative specifications are never treated as independent studies. A sensitivity analysis keeps every eligible estimate and models their dependence in a multilevel model [@cheungGuideConductingMetaanalysis2019], and a Bayesian random-effects model is a second. The primary pool is restricted to samples aged 7 to 10. A moderated pool adds samples aged 11 to 18 or spanning both ranges, with the age stratum as a moderator, and its estimate is reported with Hypotheses 2 and 3 as the review's own evidence on whether text-feature effects change with age. Where the primary pool has fewer than two papers for a coefficient but the moderated pool has at least two, the moderated estimate is used and the substitution is stated. For Hypothesis 6, studies of oral reading rate enter only a sensitivity pool, because the app does not record whether a child read silently or aloud. Where a meta-analysis in the corpus subsumes three or more of the other papers, the pooled row will be preferred and those papers dropped. Otherwise, those papers will be used and the pooled row dropped. In either case, the alternative will be reported as a sensitivity analysis.

The prior is then Student's $t(3, \hat\mu, \sigma)$, where $\hat\mu$ is the pooled estimate on the model's scale and $\sigma = 2\sqrt{\mathrm{SE}(\hat\mu)^2 + \hat\tau^2}$, with a floor of 0.10. The heavy tails let the data override a misplaced centre. For each component, we will record from the pipeline's output whether $|\hat\mu|$ falls below 0.10 standard deviations, the comparison that decides whether the sixth adjustment to the main text's precision thresholds runs. The frozen rules do not contain this step, which this protocol adds. The timestamped output will be deposited before the extract is transferred. The complete prior table, forest plots, conversion arithmetic and exclusion appendix will accompany the Stage 2 report.

> 2. That extract is held by Gameloft and has not been transferred, in whole or in part, to the University of Oxford research team or to anyone acting for it.
> 3. It will be transferred only on written confirmation of in-principle acceptance.
> 4. Material shared with the team to date: a 35-row sample and the data dictionary, shared on 27 July 2026 to confirm the structure of the table; the story texts; and the counts and file record described above.
> 5. No analysis relating story text to reading time has been conducted by Gameloft or reported to the team.

> Deputy: [name, role]\
> Signed: [name, role, date]

The accompanying record in clause 1 is the manifest described under Data provenance in the main text, to be deposited on receipt as the Data availability statement sets out. The data controller will record any row removed from the held extract between the build and the transfer, as Ethics information states. The effect of any removal on the counts will be reported at Stage 2.

Clause 4 lists the 35-row structural sample, which contains real reading times. The main text discloses the sample under Pilot data, with the summary computed from it on 6 August 2026, and Section S8 reports both. The story texts in clause 4 are stimulus materials. The editorial office confirmed in advance that such materials may be received before submission, for the reasons given under Data provenance in the main text.

Clause 5 is consistent with the published descriptive analysis of an earlier window of this platform [@ratnerProductiveStruggleChildrens2026]. That analysis draws on summaries the data controller prepared and reports completion, disengagement, scaffold use and the marginal distribution of the difficulty rating. It relates no property of a story to any behavioural measure and analyses no reading duration.

None of the four hypotheses set out under Contingent hypotheses in the main text is activated at submission. The data controller has not confirmed that post-story responses include comprehension items. It has stated that the classic stories were created with the same generative model as the others, which rules out the condition of contingent hypothesis C4. Any written confirmation would be reproduced here, as would the provider-computed counts of accounts that switched narration and the revised script's count of sessions whose account identifier is in floating-point notation.

## Counts made on the story texts before acceptance

This record lists every count made on the story texts before in-principle acceptance, with its date, what it produced and the decisions it informed. None involves an outcome. The extraction script listed under Code availability in the main text, run on the deliveries of 1 and 26 October 2026, counted the pages and whitespace-separated tokens of every text. The published tables carry both counts, from which the pages per hundred words that will enter a registered sensitivity refit can be approximated. The script lists structurally unusual texts, which we examined to draw up questions for the data controller, and removes none. On 1 October, we also identified in the catalogue the texts behind the structural sample's stories and compared their page counts with those the sample records.

On 26 October, the script also produced the structural counts reported under Materials in the main text and flagged as repetitive any text whose zlib compression ratio is below half its language's median. We set that threshold after computing every text's ratio, and it flags six Hebrew texts in which a short sequence repeats over and over. Exclusion will be decided after acceptance by the anomaly battery under Outcome-neutral quality checks, whose check for repeated loops is separate from this flag. Also on 26 October, the letters of 200 Serbian and 200 Kazakh texts showed that both languages were delivered in Cyrillic script. A comparison of the English texts of the two deliveries found 40,539 of the 40,559 identical once the line-break escapes were decoded. On 28 October, we classified how each English page ends, to prepare questions for the data controller. In 214 stories, the text ends without closing punctuation or on a cut-off page marker. Of the pages before the last, 107 in 105 stories end without closing punctuation, and the page after 39 of them continues in lower case. These counts anticipate the report, registered under Sensitivity analyses, of how pagination aligns with sentence ends. The checks kept no per-text value beyond the published counts and the lists of flagged texts, and none of them changed a registered rule.

The remaining counts served planning. On 20 October 2026, a script counted words, characters, pages and sentence-end marks in the English texts of the first delivery. It kept no per-text value and printed corpus totals, percentiles of words and characters per text, and the mean, median and maximum words per text by story type and reading level. Its 7.1 words per sentence-end mark and 6.0 characters per word, spaces and punctuation included, are corpus-level analogues of the registered mean sentence length and mean orthographic length. These figures sized the computation planned after acceptance. The text lengths they showed also led us to widen the theory object's scope from texts of 200 to 400 words to texts of 200 to 600.

In the benchmarks on public text, the median of 413 words per text set the length of the texts built by sampling, joining or cutting public material. The benchmarks that use such texts include those that estimate the error model's constants, forecast which languages pass the reliability floor and score the segmentation reported under Materials. The median is also the length at which the expected effects of connective density and referential overlap were computed (Section S5) and at which split-half reliabilities were projected. Some split-half reliabilities were also projected to 513 words, the mean length of the oldest level's generated texts. The ratio of 7.1 set the sentence lengths in two benchmark conditions, an encoder timing and a sentence-splitting test whose result was later set aside. It also supported giving surprisal a context longer than a single sentence. With the 5th percentile of 310 words per text, it suggested that the registered five-sentence floor would remove almost no generated text, and the floor was kept.

On 2 November, we counted the pages of each English text of the second delivery and the whitespace-separated tokens and characters on each page, and kept that per-text table outside the repository. On 3 November, we summed the published page and token counts in eight languages to size the computation for Bulgarian, Hungarian, Kazakh and Serbian. The same day, the per-text counts of 2 November were used to simulate matching public stories to the catalogue's text lengths. They also served to trial, on 2,000 of the texts, a public stand-in corpus with the catalogue's page structure. The full stand-in, on which the feature pipeline will be tested, will be built from the same counts before acceptance. Any further count made before acceptance will be added to this record.

# S8. The structural sample

This section reports in full the 35-row structural sample and the summary computed from it, both described under Pilot data in the main text, and cites the data dictionary where it defines a field. All 35 sessions were finished readings, with the last page reached equal to the page count, so the extract is a record of completed readings. The age band was blank in 10 sessions, and the recorded bands skewed towards children under 7, with only six sessions at 7 to 8 and two at 9 and over. The inclusion criterion of 7 and over is therefore expected to remove a substantial share of the extract. The per-session activity counters summed to more than the recorded reading time in 6 of the 14 sessions with any activity, so they are set aside under question (b) in Table 2 of the main text.

@tbl-sample-fields tabulates the 35 rows by field, and @tbl-sample-timing reproduces the reading-time check from the summary the count script wrote on 6 August 2026. The script is deposited in `count_script/`, both in the version supplied on 7 August 2026, which wrote that summary, and in a revised version dated 17 September 2026 and supplied on 18 September. Re-running either version on the sample reproduces that summary line for line, apart from the date of the run and, for the revised version, its version number and the seventeen rows it adds. @tbl-sample-timing can be regenerated from either version's output, as can most entries of @tbl-sample-fields. The script does not report the rating categories, the two title values, the sessions per text, the number of distinct timestamps or whether reading times are whole numbers. Those entries, the three activity-counter rows and the comparison of those counters with the recorded reading time were tallied directly from the sample.

In the sample, the account identifier was written in floating-point notation with six significant digits, the form a spreadsheet gives a nineteen-digit integer. The 35 values are distinct at that precision. A full extract written the same way, however, could not be relied on to distinguish accounts, so the identifier's format matters for the transfer.
